articles.title: Can AI break encryption? OpenAI’s new math has cryptographers divided
articles.author: Chris Stokel-Walker
articles.content:
Last week OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, dropped 722 mathematical manuscripts online in one go, every one of them penned by an artificial intelligence model unavailable to the public. The output was far from perfect: OpenAI withdrew three of the papers within a day, and mathematicians are still poring over the rest. But the scale of the research, and the incisiveness of its insights, has some worried.
Math powers cryptography. Every text you send and every bank log-in you submit is protected by a math problem that’s supposedly impossible to crack. The system rests on the assumption that no one will figure out how. And AI just showed it’s pretty good at math.
That worries Matthew Green, a cryptographer at Johns Hopkins University. In a social media post a few days after OpenAI’s massive math release, he suggested there was a 15 percent chance that we could lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms—which allow computers to establish secure connections and verify digital identities without first exchanging a shared secret key.

That confidence comes from decades of failed attempts to break those algorithms. Take elliptic curve cryptography, used across the Internet and by cryptocurrencies. Its security relies on the belief that there’s no efficient algorithm capable of reversing the mathematical operations at its core. But if AI can spot shortcuts that humans have missed, that belief could be proven wrong.
Humans have found such shortcuts before, Green says. An algorithm called the number field sieve made it far easier to crack RSA, another widely used public-key system, when it relied on 512-bit keys. Cryptographers responded by lengthening the keys, and 2,048 bits is now considered the minimum. Another advance on that scale “could potentially seriously reduce the security level of the schemes that we standardize,” he says.
Govind Pimpale, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, thinks AI could make the next one more likely. Public-key cryptography depends on relatively few mathematical problems, he says, each studied by a comparatively small community. Machines could throw vastly more effort at them and find flaws or faster algorithms that would let attackers work out secret keys from public ones. “Public-key cryptography is necessary for essentially all online commerce and secure messaging, so its loss would have dire consequences,” he says.
Plenty of others disagree that AI will break modern encryption. Yehuda Lindell, a professor at Bar-Ilan University in Israel and head of cryptography at Coinbase, wrote on X that there is “no evidence whatsoever” of a breakthrough against the mathematical problems underlying those systems. Nor does a single one of OpenAI’s 722 papers deal with cryptography, which Dan Boneh, a professor of computer science at Stanford University, calls “a little striking.”
Still, Green’s worry is not entirely hypothetical. In a recent preprint, Florian Tramèr, a computer scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich, and his colleagues—three of them at the AI company Anthropic—pitted leading AI models against 191 code-breaking challenges. “It’s pretty clear that models’ ability in cryptanalysis is growing extremely rapidly,” Tramèr says. In summer 2025 the researchers weren’t even sure AI could reproduce relatively simple attacks. Months later, the models were turning up weaknesses no one had spotted before. Anthropic has also reported that its Claude model found a substantially improved attack on HAWK, a proposed digital signature scheme designed to withstand quantum computers.
But there’s a huge gulf between finding weaknesses in experimental cryptography and breaking the systems that secure large parts of our digital lives. “Today no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI,” Pimpale concedes. The bigger concern is a shortcut that cracks an entire family of mathematical problems at once, and with it every system built on them.
Public-key cryptography secures the connection between your browser and the sites you visit, and it produces the digital signatures that certify a software update or a cryptocurrency transaction. Crack it, and attackers could pose as your bank or listen in on your messages. Anyone who has stockpiled encrypted traffic could go back and read it years after the senders assumed it was safe.
Even then, it wouldn’t necessarily signal disaster. Bart Preneel, a cryptography professor at the Catholic University of Leuven (KU Leuven) in Belgium, says the consequences would depend on the scale of any breakthrough. A modest mathematical advance might dent the protection offered by existing systems but not break it. Even making an attack a billion times faster might still leave it requiring more computing power than anyone could realistically muster, AI or no AI. “I think there is, at least at this moment, no real reason to panic,” he says.
Even a modest advance would necessitate a defense upgrade, and Green thinks that that could do damage of its own. “The upgrade process itself is going to be a bit of a catastrophe,” he says. “We screw up the upgrade, and we end up with something insecure accidentally.”
Eyal Ronen, a researcher at Tel Aviv University, who co-authored the cryptanalysis study, is, like Preneel, cautious. AI is already very good at finding software vulnerabilities, he says, which presents a much more immediate threat than the hypothetical disappearance of encryption. And any hacker is more likely to take the easier route, such as hacking someone’s computer to steal their encryption keys, than to try breaking the mathematics protecting them.
Efforts to prepare for quantum computers, another potential threat, are already forcing governments and companies to rethink their encryption. Boneh says those efforts could help if AI discovers something unexpected, although the two threats aren’t identical. HAWK, after all, was built for the quantum era, yet AI found a way to weaken it.
For now, Boneh wants something relatively straightforward from AI companies: greater transparency about what their models have tried and how often they’ve succeeded. Green agrees. “We’re getting no signal whatsoever,” he says. If the labs have pointed their models at the mathematical problems underpinning cryptography, saying so would help reassure the people responsible for securing the Internet. “Please tell us what you have discovered when you tried some cryptography questions,” Boneh says. Until someone does, nobody can say whether AI has exposed something fundamental about the mathematics we rely on—or whether it’s simply getting better at solving problems that were always solvable.
articles.summary:
OpenAI recently released 722 mathematical manuscripts generated by artificial intelligence, sparking expert debate over whether advanced models could eventually compromise the encryption systems securing global digital communications.

### Key Points
- OpenAI published 722 AI-generated math papers, though three were retracted shortly after release due to inaccuracies.
- Cryptographers like Matthew Green warn that AI could potentially identify mathematical shortcuts, threatening the security of public-key encryption algorithms.
- Research from ETH Zurich and Anthropic shows AI models are rapidly improving at cryptanalysis, including finding weaknesses in quantum-resistant schemes like HAWK.
- Experts like Yehuda Lindell and Bart Preneel argue there is currently no evidence that AI has broken any widely deployed cryptographic standards.
- Security professionals emphasize that stealing encryption keys remains a more immediate and practical threat than the theoretical mathematical collapse of encryption.

### Why it Matters
Public-key cryptography serves as the foundation for secure online commerce, banking, and private messaging. If AI models successfully discover fundamental mathematical flaws, it could force a massive, high-risk global infrastructure upgrade to protect sensitive digital data.

articles.title: Inside the race to train robots on human work
articles.author: rjetha@businessinsider.com (Rya Jetha)
articles.content:
One Friday evening this summer, a private chef prepared a three-course meal — burrata salad, baked salmon, and tiramisu — for two friends and me.
The dinner was free, but there was a catch. A camera mounted on Chef Aliser Demir's baseball cap was recording everything.
Demir came to my apartment through Shift, the data-collection arm of the German startup Microagi. The startup offers free private chefs in San Francisco in exchange for first-person footage of their work. Shift offered to pay Demir, who runs a private chef business, his usual rate of $100 to $150 per person.
"I've been feeding people since I started this job," Demir said. "Now I am also feeding AI."
Demir is part of a global effort to collect data on how humans interact with the physical world, with the goal of building machines that can staff factories, clean homes, and even fight wars. Elon Musk, who is betting Tesla's future on the humanoid robot Optimus, has promoted a utopian future of "sustainable abundance," in which AI and robots make human labor largely optional.
For now, those ambitions face a problem: a massive shortage of training data. "It is widely agreed in the robotics world that data is the key bottleneck," said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies technology and industrial policy.
This is the third installment of the AI Data Grab, Business Insider's series on how human work is becoming raw material for AI — and the companies that are cashing in. So far, we've reported on how AI labs are buying up employees' emails and Slack messages, and how law firms are turning decades of human expertise into AI systems. Now, the scramble is moving into the physical world, where companies are paying people to record skills robots have yet to learn.
Contract workers in Mexico and the Philippines remotely control robots in American warehouses as they pack beauty products, recording movements so the machines can eventually do the work on their own. Other workers across the world strap cameras to their foreheads to capture first-person footage of themselves folding laundry and making hotel beds.
"This is how the great knowledge transfer happens from humans to robots," said Josh Gruenstein, CEO of Tutor Intelligence. His company operates a Massachusetts "data factory" where workers remotely control robots to generate training data.
A booming data market
Demand for robot training data is roughly 10 times higher than a year ago, Vineeth Velmurugan, who leads robot learning at the AI data startup Encord, said. Encord's customers, including Dyna Robotics and Agility Robotics, once requested 1,000 hours of annotated data. Now they want 10,000 or even 100,000, he said.
That red-hot demand for real-world data comes as robotics has become one of Silicon Valley's hottest bets. Humanoid robot makers Figure AI and Agility Robotics have fetched multibillion-dollar valuations, as have the companies developing robot "brains" such as Skild AI and Physical Intelligence.
Robotics companies raised $33.4 billion globally in the first half of this year, according to PitchBook data, surpassing the $28.7 billion raised in all of 2025. Cheaper hardware and computing, better AI models, labor shortages, and competition with China are all fueling investor interest.
But a gulf remains between robots that perform impressive demos and machines reliable enough to work an eight-hour factory shift. Robotics companies hope more training data will help, and suppliers across the world, from scrappy startups to established companies like Scale AI, Instawork, and Uber, are rushing to sell it to them.
Custom hardware is key to recording the physical world. Mecka AI, which has raised more than $120 million from investors including Sequoia and Nvidia, started with an app that paid people to record everyday activities two years ago. But the company soon ran into the limits of ordinary video.
Mecka now designs headgear and sensor-equipped gloves to "sensorize humans," CEO Josh Gao said. The equipment records movements and force, such as the pressure needed to grip a glass or crack an egg. Contractors label workplace footage before Mecka sells it to AI labs and robotics companies.
Microagi, the parent company of Shift, is expanding its collection efforts into homes and workplaces across more than 15 countries. It pays more than 35,000 people to record themselves performing physical tasks, CEO Bercan Kilic said. Shift said participants can earn up to $30 an hour and that it has paid out around $10 million in 2026.
Household chores are the most common, but unusual tasks help expose models to unfamiliar situations. One contributor in Turkey records himself repairing old jet engines in his garage, Kilic said.
Kilic's goal is to gather enough data to build robots that can work in factories and address labor shortages in Europe and the US. "If you run factories, the math is already on your desk," Kilic previously told Business Insider. "Your most experienced people retire this decade, and their replacements were never born. Reshoring only works if the robots do."
Income today, automation tomorrow
For the workers supplying that data, though, the trade-off is income today in exchange for helping build machines that could eventually automate their work.
Demir, the private chef, said he believes his work is safe. "Machines can just watch, listen, and follow instructions," he said. "They cannot feel or smell."
The economics are different in countries where labor is cheaper. Human Archive, a data collection company based in San Francisco, began building operations in India last year through partnerships with gig platforms, hotels, and plumbing and electrical businesses. It started with an app that let people record audio and first-person video. The startup now also makes custom hardware in China, including camera-equipped headsets and wrist trackers that capture movement.
Today, it operates in more than 30 countries and pays workers between $1 to $10 and "even much more," per hour, depending on how disruptive the equipment is, CEO Raj Patel said. These workers, Patel said, could earn "almost as much, or more [than their regular jobs], to just wear these devices."
Mecka and Human Archive did not say how they ensure workers' consent when collecting data through partner businesses or local contractors. Shift said participation is voluntary, and some employees at partner businesses choose not to participate. The company said it obtains explicit consent, explaining what data is collected and how it is used, including that it may be licensed to other labs for AI and robotics training.
The global competition for data work can come with a downside. It drives down wages and leaves workers with little bargaining power, said Mark Graham, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute and author of Feeding the Machine, a book about the labor behind AI. "Often the workers don't even know what they're doing," he said. "They're a very disposable appendage of a much bigger machine."
The work can also be physically taxing. One operator who remotely controls robots in US warehouses from a Texas facility previously told Business Insider that eight-hour shifts cause arm and shoulder cramps. "We even have a massage gun in the office," they said.
Will the data boom last?
The companies collecting all this data are betting that the quest to train intelligent robots will fuel demand for years to come. Research firm Mordor Intelligence projects that the broader AI training dataset market will grow from $11.9 billion this year to nearly $49.8 billion by 2031.
For robotics data suppliers, the bull case is that startups will spend a significant share of their funding on training material, said Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners.
"If scaling laws continue to work, the pie will just keep growing," he said.
But nobody knows how much data robots will need to work reliably, he added. If they need less than expected, data suppliers could lose business. If they need much more, investors could tire of paying before the robots become commercially viable.
Some are betting that demand for robot training data is nowhere near its peak. Encord's Velmurugan likens today's robot brain to that of a two-year-old, and estimates that training a robot to work in homes — one of the hardest environments because it is so unstructured — could require a dataset five times the size of YouTube. At the end of 2025, YouTube held an estimated 29 billion videos, the equivalent of 280,000 years of footage, according to research firm Omdia.
"It's hard to say how this will play out," Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley robotics professor and cofounder of warehouse robotics startup Ambi Robotics, said. "It might take five years or 50 years. And even if we had unlimited data now, I don't know if this approach will work," he said.
Training robots in virtual environments, known as simulation, could also change the equation. World Labs, a startup slated for an $8.2 billion acquisition by AMD, says it can turn a small set of recordings into simulated environments and modify them to generate more training data for robots. If the technology delivers, robotics companies could need far less data from the physical world.
But even sustained demand doesn't guarantee a profitable business.
Earlier this year, Sam Padilla shut down his robotics data startup, Eidon AI, after struggling with logistics, upfront costs, and thin margins. He compared the business to dropshipping, where retailers sell goods shipped directly by suppliers and pocket the markup — until competitors offering the same products for less squeeze their margins.
"There is a clear arbitrage opportunity to make money if you're willing to race and race to the bottom," he said. "But a technical bottleneck does not necessarily imply a good business."

articles.summary:
Startups are paying thousands of workers globally to record their daily physical tasks, creating massive datasets intended to train humanoid robots for future labor in homes and factories.

### Key Points
- Companies like Microagi, Mecka AI, and Human Archive use head-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves to capture human movements, force, and physical interactions.
- Demand for robot training data has surged tenfold in the past year, with robotics firms seeking up to 100,000 hours of annotated footage to improve machine reliability.
- Global data collection efforts span over 30 countries, with workers performing tasks ranging from cooking and cleaning to repairing jet engines.
- The AI training dataset market is projected to grow from $11.9 billion this year to nearly $49.8 billion by 2031.
- Robotics companies raised $33.4 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by investor interest in automating labor and addressing workforce shortages.

### Why it Matters
The race to build functional humanoid robots is currently bottlenecked by a lack of real-world training data, turning human labor into a critical commodity for AI development. While this creates immediate income for global workers, it simultaneously accelerates the automation of the very tasks they are being paid to record.

articles.title: Secret documents reveal donors behind $330 million for Trump's ballroom
articles.author: Jonathan O'Connell,Sarah Blaskey and Aaron Schaffer, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
articles.content:
A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump's White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member.
Tech giants Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million, the top contribution amount, the list shows. The Adelson family, one of the GOP's largest donor dynasties, committed that sum as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network.
Absent from the list is Trump himself, who has said that he is helping to pay for the project. "It's being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine," he said last year, days after demolition began on the old East Wing.
The White House publicly identified 37 people, companies and foundations as donors last October, without revealing the amount of their individual gifts.
The list obtained by The Post, an internal spreadsheet used to track contributions for the fundraising effort, contains the source, date and amount of all 67 donations above $10,000 recorded as of late last month. It shows a total of $333 million from private donors, aligning with the administration's public statements. Additional records, also internal to the fundraising effort, provide more detail about the donations and indicate that at least $77 million came from donors who requested anonymity.
The list and other documents offer a panoramic view of a fundraising campaign that is extraordinary both for its size and opacity. Ordinary political giving requires public disclosure and is subject to campaign finance rules. The ballroom donations are collected by a nonprofit and then channeled to the government and into a White House account the president directly controls.
Independent experts and scholars have expressed alarm at the potential the arrangement has for influence buying and coerced giving.
Some donors on the list obtained by The Post cut large checks, while others created installment plans that are still being paid off, the additional records show. The list does not include in-kind contributions.
The Post's reporting does not establish a connection between the donation commitments and favorable actions by the Trump administration. But the documents show that the vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government.
Companies or executives of firms that have had contracts with the federal government during Trump's second term accounted for about half of the total, The Post found.
After reviewing the list obtained by The Post, White House spokesman Davis Ingle declined to discuss individual donations but described the ballroom donors as "a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People's House better for generations to come."
"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," he said. He added that the administration will "relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give."
The Post is publishing the names of the 57 donors listed as having committed to giving $100,000 or more. The additional records detailing donors' preferences show at least nine wanted to remain anonymous.
The Post attempted to reach all the donors whose names appear in this report. Most did not respond or declined to comment. Those who did comment said that there was no connection between their donations and any favorable government actions.
Nvidia, the world's most valuable public company, became a top contributor to the ballroom in October 2025, nearly three months after it struck a groundbreaking pact with Trump to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns.
CEO Jensen Huang told reporters at the time that the company was contributing to Trump's ballroom "in a small way" but did not provide a dollar amount. Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous.
"As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in response to questions from The Post. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made."
Major GOP donor Joseph Popolo Jr., Trump's ambassador to the Netherlands, and his wife contributed $1 million from their family fund to support the ballroom project in late 2025, the records show. Their donation - made two months after Popolo's confirmation - has not been previously reported.
Trump Cabinet member Kelly Loeffler of the Small Business Administration and her husband Jeff Sprecher, former chairman of the New York Stock Exchange, promised $5 million for the project, the list shows. Brandon Lutnick, chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald and the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, donated stock worth more than $2.5 million, the records show.
Popolo, Loeffler, Sprecher and the Lutnicks did not respond to requests for comment.
More than three-quarters of the money for the ballroom came in commitments of $5 million or more. Among the top donors are some of America's blue-chip companies, including Amazon, Caterpillar, Comcast, Microsoft and T-Mobile. (Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos owns The Post.)
Cryptocurrency companies, now under loosened regulations from the Trump administration, and their investors promised more than $18 million. The largest portion came from Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss, co-founders of the Gemini crypto exchange, who together donated bitcoin valued at $5,050,018, the records show.
The Winklevoss brothers did not respond to requests for comment.
The ballroom project has also received dozens of small contributions, some as low as $10. The list and additional documents show the source of all but $24,000 of the total donations.
The total fundraising amount falls short of the $400 million Trump has said he intends to raise for the work. The cost of building the new East Wing, which includes the ballroom, office space and an underground military facility, was projected in March to have increased to $600 million, an estimate previously reported by The Post. The White House has used taxpayer dollars to cover some of the construction cost, records show.
The ballroom donations are routed through the Trust for the National Mall, a D.C.-based nonprofit whose mission is to restore and preserve the National Mall and the White House grounds. Nonprofits are not generally required to disclose their donors.
Prospective donors were sent a "pledge agreement form," a copy of which was obtained by The Post, for giving toward the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom." The form lists Meredith O'Rourke, the top fundraiser for Trump's 2024 campaign, as the main contact.
O'Rourke referred questions to the White House.
A 12-page agreement between the government and the Trust requires that the Trust "maintain the anonymity of Project donors to the extent provided by law and not publicly recognize any such donor unless explicitly authorized in writing" by staff in the White House's Executive Residence unit.
Democratic lawmakers have denounced the fundraising for the ballroom as secretive and potentially transactional. They have demanded that the administration and the Trust provide details about the donors and circumstances of the gifts. Those demands have been rebuffed.
In a statement the Trust said: "In philanthropy, it is not uncommon for donors to request their gifts remain anonymous. The Trust is committed to honoring donors requesting anonymity."
Pardon for international banker
One of the earliest commitments to donate to the ballroom, from Sept. 23, 2025, came from the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, an international banker and dual Venezuelan-Italian citizen.
In 2022, the Justice Department indicted Herrera Velutini, then 50, on bribery charges, accusing him of helping finance the campaign of Puerto Rico's then-governor in exchange for the removal of a regulator investigating his bank. The former governor and a political consultant were also charged.
Herrera Velutini and his attorney unsuccessfully tried to get the case dismissed, claiming prosecutors were criminalizing lawful political activity.
After Trump's victory, Herrera's daughter, Isabela Herrera, made two donations to Trump's MAGA Inc., a political action committee, totaling $3.5 million, campaign finance records show.
The donations prompted the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center to file a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging that Isabela Herrera was serving as a "straw donor" for her father. The organization described her as a self-employed financial consultant in her mid-20s whose only prior political donation was $20 to Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic presidential candidate.
The organization said it got no response from the FEC, which declined to comment for this story.
In August 2025, Herrera Velutini's charges were reduced to a misdemeanor as part of a plea agreement.
The following month, Isabela Herrera committed to donating $2.5 million for the ballroom, which has not been previously reported. Records show she paid a first installment of $835,000 on Oct. 14, 2025. Trump pardoned Herrera Velutini in January. Herrera's second payment was due this month, the records show.
Amid a wider Justice Department retreat from sweeping public corruption investigations, Trump also pardoned the former governor and the political consultant. The White House said the prosecutions had been politically motivated.
After the pardon, an attorney for Herrera Velutini issued a statement saying his client was "profoundly grateful to President Donald J. Trump for bestowing the grace of his benevolent pardon."
Neither Herrera Velutini nor his daughter responded to requests for comment.
A dropped investigation
Last year, Ergen, the telecommunications executive, found his company EchoStar in the Trump administration's crosshairs.
Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, wrote Ergen in May to inform him that the agency had begun investigating EchoStar. Carr threatened to yank government licenses that were critical to the survival of the business, accusing EchoStar, owner of Dish Network, of not following through on promises it had made to upgrade its cellphone network.
The following month, Ergen met with Trump and Carr behind closed doors to discuss the investigation, according to Bloomberg. The outlet, citing unnamed sources, said the June 11 discussion included a brief exchange about Ergen's political donations and whether he gave to candidates in both political parties.
The company referenced a June 11 meeting between Ergen and Carr in a regulatory filing and wrote that Trump "subsequently encouraged the parties involved to reach an amicable resolution."
Ergen negotiated a deal to sell some of the company's licenses to AT&T in August, subject to approval of the FCC and Justice Department.
Carr dropped the investigation the following month, thanking Ergen for his responses and for information he had provided.
In December, with the sale still pending, Ergen committed $12.5 million to Trump's ballroom, according to the donation list. Records indicate Ergen requested that the source of the donation remain anonymous. The donation has not been previously reported.
He committed another $12.5 million in February, according to the list.
In May, the FCC and the Justice Department each gave EchoStar approval for the sale.
Through a spokesman, Ergen and EchoStar declined to comment. The FCC and Carr did not respond. DOJ did not provide comment for this story.
The donor list also shows $5 million "pledged" by AT&T, the only line item on the list described that way. Every other amount is listed as "won."
In a statement to The Post, AT&T spokesperson Megan Ketterer said the company appeared to have been listed in error. "We have no idea what list you are talking about and have no plans to contribute to the Trust for the National Mall," Ketterer said.
An approval, then a donation
Another top donor was a subsidiary of Rocket, the Detroit-based housing, finance and tech company founded by Daniel Gilbert, owner of the NBA's Cleveland Cavaliers.
In March 2025, Rocket said that it planned to acquire two competitors: the home search site Redfin and the mortgage site Mr. Cooper. The moves would give Rocket a much larger share of the real estate market.
Federal agencies tasked with protecting against anticompetitive business practices declined to challenge the deals, allowing them to proceed. Five Democratic senators wrote to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission in protest.
To acquire Mr. Cooper, Gilbert also needed approval from the Federal Housing Finance Agency.
The FHFA approved the deal on Aug. 26, 2025.
The Rocket subsidiary committed $10 million to the ballroom three weeks later. Records show it requested anonymity.
A Rocket spokesperson said the approvals and donation were not connected.
"Rocket and its related companies have supported the Trust for the National Mall and other nonpartisan organizations in Washington for more than a decade," said spokesperson Aaron Emerson. "We're proud to join dozens of companies and individuals in improving our nation's capital."
An FTC spokesperson said Rocket received no special treatment, pointing to a lawsuit the agency brought against Redfin for anticompetitive practices days after the donation.
The FHFA and the Justice Department did not provide comment.
Software contracts
One of the country's leading software providers, Salesforce, has significantly grown its government contracting business during the second Trump administration.
Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff has attended exclusive dinners and events with Trump, including a state dinner hosted by King Charles III at Windsor Castle in September 2025 and a business summit in Japan the following month. While there, Trump thanked Benioff for previously putting him on the cover of Time magazine, which Benioff owns.
"Marc has some pretty good suggestions," Trump said of the CEO.
The following day, Benioff committed $1 million to the ballroom, according to the list. The donation has not previously been reported, and Benioff asked that it remain anonymous.
Salesforce separately made two $1 million commitments to the ballroom, one last Christmas Eve and another Jan. 29 of this year, the list shows. The donations have not been previously reported.
In between, the Army awarded the company a contract worth up to $5.6 billion through 2035, which appears to be the largest public government contract in Salesforce's history, according to a review of public contracting records. Announcing the contract, the Pentagon said "bids were solicited via the internet with only one received."
Benioff and Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.
In a statement, a Pentagon official said: "Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding decisions."
After this article published, an Army spokesperson said in a statement that contracts are awarded in strict compliance with federal law and are "determined exclusively by validated mission requirements, technical capability, and best value."
One of Salesforce's competitors, ServiceNow, also donated to the ballroom.
Last September, the General Services Administration announced what it called a "landmark" agreement with ServiceNow that would make the company's AI-driven software available to federal agencies at a discount.
"When President Trump says the federal government needs to operate like a best-run business, he means it," CEO Bill McDermott said as part of the announcement.
The next month, ServiceNow committed $5 million to the ballroom, a donation that has not been previously reported.
The GSA said in a statement that ServiceNow has been a federal contractor for more than a decade, adding that "its charitable or political donations - like those of any company - have no bearing on GSA's decision to include them in federal buying catalogs."
ServiceNow said in a statement that negotiations for the deal had been underway for a "considerable period of time." Its government business is "separate and unconnected to any donations we make to any cause," it said.
Of the donation, the company said: "Many of our partners and peers were also contributing to the project. We chose to join them."
Venezuelan oil interests
Nearly $10 million for the ballroom was committed by two Trump political donors who have pursued large investments in Venezuelan oil - a market Trump has gained influence over since the U.S. seizure of President Nicolás Maduro in January.
Billionaire financier Paul Singer committed to donate $5 million through his foundation in October 2025, a month before his hedge fund received court approval to pursue a purchase of Venezuelan oil giant Citgo for $5.9 billion.
The deal will require approval from multiple federal agencies, including the Commerce Department, Energy Department, State Department and Treasury Department. It has stalled amid ongoing negotiations with the South American country's U.S.-backed administration.
The Oklahoma oil and gas company Continental Resources and its chairman emeritus, billionaire and GOP megadonor Harold Hamm, both promised donations to the ballroom in October 2025 totaling just under $5 million.
This year, in response to the Trump administration's call for energy companies to invest in the Venezuelan oil industry, Continental struck a tentative agreement with the country's state-run oil company to develop 126,000 acres of untapped oil fields.
Singer declined to comment. Neither Hamm nor Continental responded.
Unlisted
Two companies and one individual the White House has publicly named as donors do not appear on the list obtained by The Post.
The companies are Hard Rock International, the hospitality chain owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, and Tether America, a cryptocurrency firm. The individual is Paolo Tiramani, a modular homes company executive who told the Times of London that he had donated $10 million in stock.
None of the three answered The Post's questions or explained why they are not recorded as having contributed to the ballroom fundraising campaign. Neither did the Trust for the National Mall or the White House.
Kevin Crowe, Samantha Schmidt, Dan Lamothe and Alex Horton contributed to this report.

articles.title: An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
articles.author: Emma Roth
articles.content:
An Israeli ad tech firm worked with spyware companies to infect devices, including at Al Jazeera, by simply showing users an online ad, according to a joint investigation by security researchers at Citizen Lab and Confiant. It’s the first time researchers have found technical evidence of a zero-click attack — a form of hacking that requires no action by users — delivered through targeted advertising, as reported earlier by NBC News.
An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
It’s the first time researchers found evidence of a zero-click attack delivered through targeted advertising.
The ad firm, called Discover-Tech, presents itself as a typical online advertising agency, but researchers say it actually provides a pipeline for hacking groups to plant malicious ads across the web. It operates a platform known as “Controlium” that allows its spyware partners to “precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking,” according to the investigation. It also allows them to “select a user for infection or profiling” using their IP address, mobile ad ID, or browser identifier.
One of the groups Discover-Tech works with is Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that has been blacklisted by the US government. In 2024 and 2025, Discover-Tech ads delivered Candiru-linked spyware to Al Jazeera, a Qatar-based news network. Researchers say the companies targeted “at least” 45 devices at the news outlet in 2024 and 2025.
Citizen Lab and Confiant call on the advertising industry to ramp up security on their platforms. Google and the Comcast-owned advertising company Beeswax have since removed Discover-Tech from their platforms, while IAB Europe suspended the company from its list of approved vendors, Reuters reports. Researchers also recommend that users at high risk of targeting use ad blockers, disable ad tracking, and regularly reset mobile ad IDs.

- The investigation linked Discover-Tech to the blacklisted spyware firm Candiru, which targeted at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera during 2024 and 2025.

- Experts recommend that high-risk users mitigate these threats by utilizing ad blockers, disabling ad tracking, and regularly resetting their mobile advertising identifiers.

### Why it Matters
This discovery marks the first documented instance of zero-click hacking delivered through the global digital advertising ecosystem, exposing a significant vulnerability in online ad infrastructure. It highlights the urgent need for stricter security vetting of ad tech vendors to prevent malicious actors from weaponizing standard web advertising networks.

articles.title: The Plot to Delete Democracy
articles.source: The New York Review of Books
articles.author: Sue Halpern
articles.content:
Chances are you already know some random things about the Silicon Valley technology billionaires who have embraced—and been embraced by—the Trump administration: that, for example, Peter Thiel’s data mining company, Palantir, supplies surveillance software to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the recent public stock offering for SpaceX briefly made Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire, or that the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, a former Democratic Party stalwart, turned to Trump after he saw, he said, the most successful people sending “their kids to the most politically radical institutions, which teach them how to be America-hating communists.” You may even know that Thiel, in contrast to most of his Silicon Valley peers, supported Trump’s 2016 campaign, or that during the 2024 campaign Musk was Trump’s largest individual donor, giving $239 million to his pro-Trump America PAC and around $50 million to other Trump-aligned groups, or that Andreessen helped staff the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), Musk’s predatory duchy within Trump’s second administration.
Yet in the fractured attention economy in which we all now reside, it’s easy to know these disparate facts and still have only a vague understanding of their larger significance. It is the mastery of such diverse particulars that makes Gil Durán’s new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, so valuable. Durán, the former editorial page editor of the San Francisco Examiner, has taken a tremendous amount of previously reported information that, on its own, might have looked like dots on a pointillist’s canvas, and created a haunting picture of the political project pursued and abetted by a confederacy of Silicon Valley elites. Their goal is nothing less than to destroy liberal democracy. Their money, in tandem with a Republican Party establishment that shares many of their objectives and a president with an insatiable lust for riches, has pushed a fringe ideology—what is popularly called technofascism but is closer in aspiration to straight-up totalitarianism—into the affairs of state.
Democracy has always been vulnerable to capture by those who would use its own apparatus to undermine it. While the United States has long harbored people and parties that have espoused antidemocratic sentiments—the Know-Nothing and Communist parties come to mind—the Supreme Court’s 2010 ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission presented an unprecedented opportunity for those willing to spend whatever it takes to elect politicians to do their bidding. According to a report by the Roosevelt Institute,
The 2024 federal elections saw the highest level of billionaire spending in American history. In an effort to influence outcomes, billionaire donors and their families spent over $2.6 billion—a figure amounting to nearly 20 percent of total federal election spending that cycle.
Most of this money went to support Donald Trump’s reelection. Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act then rewarded his billionaire friends (as well as his own family) with enormous tax cuts. But Trump’s Silicon Valley backers, who together donated nearly $400 million to his campaign, wanted something more: for the newly reelected president to demolish the federal bureaucracy and its pesky regulatory regime.
Decimating the so-called administrative state has long been advocated by right-wing partisans. In his 1981 inaugural address, for example, Ronald Reagan vowed to “curb the size and influence of the Federal establishment,” and the following year he convened the Grace Commission to root out “government waste.” (It did not, as Congress failed to implement most of its recommendations.) Twelve years later the Republican campaign platform Contract with America promised to “transform the way Congress works,” which “would be the end of government that is too big, too intrusive, and too easy with the public’s money.” Though Republicans were able to win a majority in the House—their first in forty years—their ambitions were largely stymied by a resistant Senate and the veto power of the Democratic president, Bill Clinton.
In 2024 Musk, fresh from pulverizing Twitter and imbued with the “move fast and break things” ethos of Silicon Valley, was not interested in such niceties as advisory boards or legislation. As he ingratiated himself with Trump by becoming his biggest donor, Musk pitched him on creating a strike force aimed at eliminating what he believed to be the excesses of the federal government. In keeping with the quid pro quo that has come to define Trump’s presidency, Trump issued Executive Order 14158, “Establishing and Implementing the President’s ‘Department of Government Efficiency,’” on his first day in office. And he put Musk in charge, along with the tech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy (who soon departed and is now running for governor of Ohio).
DOGE was a first run of what Durán calls “the nerd reich”: two incredibly rich guys who worship at the altar of money and technology taking an ax to federal agencies they didn’t like, such as USAID (which Musk called “a criminal organization”), slashing the budgets of the National Institutes of Health (too woke) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (whose functions, Project 2025 claimed, could be privatized and monetized), firing tens of thousands of workers, and causing hundreds of thousands of others to take buyouts or early retirement. It was disruptive, cataclysmic, and cruel—so in that sense it was a roaring success. Financially, on the other hand, it was an abject failure. Though Musk promised that DOGE would cut $2 trillion from the federal budget, not only did it not come anywhere close to that figure, its “savings claims [were] overstated, inaccurate and rooted in a fundamental misunderstanding of how the federal budget works,” according to a report by NPR, further substantiated by a recent Government Accountability Office investigation. Musk stepped down after 130 days.
Advertisement
Musk’s departure was not the end of DOGE. Russell Vought, one of the main architects of Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s blueprint for restructuring the government, whom Trump installed as director of the Office of Management and Budget, took over. A canny right-wing operative and avowed Christian nationalist who harbors a persistent disaffection for democracy, Vought was in a position to set DOGE (through the OMB) on a course to implement his vision of an autocratic, post-constitutional government. In a private speech in 2023, he said:
We want the bureaucrats to be traumatically affected. When they wake up in the morning, we want them to not want to go to work because they are increasingly viewed as the villains. We want their funding to be shut down so that the EPA can’t do all of the rules against our energy industry because they have no bandwidth financially to do so.
Vought championed what Trump called the Merit Hiring Plan, which required applicants for government vacancies to write short essays professing their patriotism and fealty to the president and his policies; seeded slash-and-burn emissaries throughout the government; and strong-armed Congress into accepting a $9.4 billion rescissions package that eliminated funding for programs maligned by the right, such as the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and the US Institute of Peace. According to a study by The American Prospect, drawing on a study by the Revolving Door Project, “DOGE was—and remains, through Vought’s OMB—an effort to extinguish the existing government and create a new one in the image of oligarchs and far-right ideologues.”
It would be inaccurate, though, to suggest that Musk’s departure from DOGE and Vought’s ascendancy represent the supremacy of the inveterate right-wing establishment over the upstart tech billionaires. Not only are the two in many ways ideologically aligned; Vought’s think tank, the Center for Renewing America, operates within a conservative ecosphere that benefits from dark money groups such as DonorsTrust and the Rockbridge Network, a “political venture capital firm” cofounded by J.D. Vance. Both DonorsTrust and Rockbridge are bankrolled in large part by Silicon Valley’s most prominent Trump supporter, the man who once famously wrote, “I no longer believe freedom and democracy are compatible”: Peter Thiel.
As Durán points out, Thiel’s politics precede Trump—indeed, they precede his own engagement with electoral politics by decades. As a Stanford undergraduate in the late 1980s he cofounded The Stanford Review as a counterweight to what he later said was the “wokeness” of the university (though the pejorative shorthand for progressive views hadn’t yet entered the right-wing lexicon). The Stanford Review attracted a group of like-minded students, many of whom later joined Thiel’s tech ventures and became very rich and aggressively doctrinal themselves.
David Sacks, for example, the editor-in-chief of The Stanford Review a few years after Thiel and the coauthor with him of the 1995 book The Diversity Myth: Multiculturalism and Political Intolerance on Campus (in which they argued, among other things, that the definition of rape had been expanded to include “seductions that are later regretted”), became an executive at Confinity, the precursor to PayPal, of which Thiel was a cofounder. When PayPal sold to eBay for $1.5 billion in 2002, he became an extremely wealthy man. Sacks is now the cochair of Trump’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, after a turn as the administration’s special adviser for AI and crypto; in that position he, among other things, worked to preempt state AI regulations. Crucially, as The New York Times reported, Sacks’s dual roles as the administration’s AI and crypto “czar,” influencing policy for both technologies while also investing in them, “laid the groundwork for his investments to flourish.”
Trump, who once called Bitcoin “a scam,” embraced cryptocurrency in his second term, creating his own crypto company with the members of his family; according to Durán, “Within a few months of his return to the White House, the Trump family’s net worth increased by $5 billion.” A recent New York Times investigation found that another crypto scheme, a Trump meme coin, netted the president hundreds of millions of dollars, while his wife took in $6 million from her cryptocurrency. In contrast, the Times noted that many of the small investors who bought these coins lost their money.
Advertisement
Beyond Trump’s self-dealing, his sudden affection for cryptocurrency has created an undetectable way for foreign nationals to ingratiate themselves with him, raising national security concerns. Consider Guren “Bobby” Zhou, a former flooring salesman and failed investor from China who had come under investigation for money laundering in the UK. Zhou put $100 million into Trump’s World Liberty Financial cryptocurrency. As the Times noted:
In any prior era, a windfall for the president of that size from a foreigner with no public signs of access to that level of wealth would have certainly gone against norms and might have spawned a congressional investigation.
Instead, the curious case of Mr. Zhou illustrates the ease with which buyers with unknown backgrounds and motivations can use the anonymity of cryptocurrency to shower Mr. Trump with money.
It remains unclear who fronted Zhou the money.
Though it may not have been obvious to the public when Thiel and his partners started Confinity, their mobile payments app PayPal was also aimed at bypassing the traditional banking system. (Confinity later merged with Musk’s digital payment platform, X.com, and took the name PayPal.) As Max Chafkin points out in his book about Thiel, The Contrarian (2021):*
From its earliest days Thiel understood that it could be a lot more than a clever way to split checks…. If it took off, it would make it impossible for governments to regulate their economies, leading to, he boasted to a reporter, “the erosion of the nation-state.”
It was the first volley in an attack on state control that almost no one buying stuff on eBay knew they were engaged in.
Durán traces Thiel’s antiestablishment heterodoxy to a 1997 book called The Sovereign Individual, written by James Dale Davidson, an American venture capitalist and the founder of the conservative National Taxpayers Union, and William Rees-Mogg, a former editor of The Times of London and a life peer in the House of Lords. The book, Durán writes,
laid out a dramatic thesis, hyping the arrival of an information age in which technology would upend both economics and politics, eliminating most jobs, reducing work to piecemeal gig assignments, and sparking widespread decline, chaos, and violence as tens of millions of people struggled to survive without work.
He continues:
Davidson and Rees-Mogg argued that technological disruption would accelerate the sorting of humanity into inferior and superior people. Their cognitive elites would be investors and tech entrepreneurs with the skills and knowledge to prosper in the new decentralized tech economy. They would become a powerful new political force, a class of “sovereign individuals” whose intelligence and wealth freed them from democracy, nationality, taxes, and regulations. “Cybercurrency”—an early term for crypto—would aid their escape and fuel their rise.
Certainly, as prescient as this seems now, it’s also possible to see the book as a formula followed by those “cognitive elites” to create the conditions to promote their domination. Bitcoin, the first mainstream cybercurrency, wasn’t “mined” until 2009, twelve years after The Sovereign Individual was published. Thiel’s Founders Fund was one of the earliest venture firms, along with Andreessen Horowitz, to invest heavily in it, thus offering Bitcoin legitimacy, which encouraged public and institutional adoption, which then increased its “value.” Both companies also hold significant amounts of Ether, the native cryptocurrency of the blockchain network Ethereum, Bitcoin’s nearest competitor. Ethereum was invented by the Russian Canadian programmer Vitalik Buterin while he was supported by the Thiel Fellowship, which rewarded young people—Buterin was twenty—with $100,000 to drop out of university or forgo it altogether to build new technologies.
Meanwhile, the gig economy Davidson and Rees-Mogg imagined came to fruition with the introduction of such platforms as Uber (2009) and Airbnb (2008), which received investments from Sacks (Uber) and Thiel (Airbnb), who were not averse to making scads of money while disempowering workers. Even the newsletter platform Substack, which established a gig economy for journalists (including Durán) just as the newspaper business was shrinking, traces its creation to the tech incubator Y Combinator, which was run by Sam Altman, the guy who keeps warning that the product being developed by his current company, OpenAI, is an existential threat to humanity or at least to workers everywhere. (Altman, who was a six-figure donor to Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential campaign but on July 4, 2025, declared himself “politically homeless,” donated $1 million to Trump’s inauguration fund and $5 million to his super PAC, MAGA Inc.) Thiel was a partner at Y Combinator at the time, and Andreessen Horowitz was one of Substack’s initial major investors. While Substack newsletters enable writers to monetize their work, they also shrink the public square—which, in Durán’s estimation, is the actual point.
Here’s Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz and the author of The Network State: How to Start a New Country (2022): “We replace media with parallel media…. They’re gaining strength. They’re pulling away users—until they become the new thing. So this is how we turn that seemingly impossible thing of building a new country.” A network state, as Srinivasan defines it, is “a highly aligned online community with a capacity for collective action that crowdfunds territory around the world and eventually gains diplomatic recognition from pre-existing states.” Or as he said on a podcast called Moment of Zen, “What I’m really calling for is something like tech Zionism.”
A more functional definition is offered by the St. Lawrence University professor Zane Griffin Talley Cooper: “The Network State model seeks to eschew most forms of social and environmental regulation, instead promoting a libertarian fantasy of rapid privatized innovation and development.” That fantasy is becoming something of a reality, thanks in part to Pronomos Capital, a venture firm run by Patri Friedman, the grandson of Milton Friedman, that supports a worldwide collection of what its website calls, with ardent vagueness, “the cities of tomorrow.” Srinivasan is an adviser to Pronomos; Thiel is an investor. (Friedman has also promoted building autonomous, extrajudicial cities floating on the ocean.)
Not long after the publication of his book, Srinivasan convened a conference in Amsterdam that highlighted network state projects already underway in San Francisco, Arizona, Texas, Honduras, and Zanzibar. There have been other conferences since; the 2025 Network State Conference attracted over eight thousand participants and featured such speakers as Buterin, Ben Horowitz, and Bryan Johnson of “Don’t Die” fame. Durán writes that a Pronomos-backed project called Praxis, led by a twenty-eight-year-old named Dryden Brown, “announced plans to build a tech city in the Mediterranean backed by Sam Altman, Joe Lonsdale, and Srinivasan himself, along with investments from Thiel and others.” (Lonsdale, another Stanford Review and PayPal alum, is a cofounder of Palantir.) It’s not clear exactly how California Forever, a real estate venture funded by a group of tech billionaires who secretly bought around 60,000 acres of land sixty miles north of San Francisco in order to build a new, improved city, fits into Srinivasan’s vision, but Durán reports that on the Moment of Zen podcast, Srinivasan “added that a major new network state project was already underway ‘on bare land’ in California,” a claim its CEO, Jan Sramek, a former Goldman Sachs trader, has denied.
Most recently, Durán reports, proponents of what are also known as “freedom cities” have been eyeing Greenland as an outpost for an unregulated tech haven where artificial intelligence and bio-hacking experiments could be developed without guardrails or government interference. In response to Trump’s interest in claiming the Danish autonomous territory for the United States, Brown tweeted:
Praxis would like to support Greenland’s development by coordinating talent, companies, and capital to help secure the Arctic, extract critical resources, terraform the land with advanced technology to make it more habitable, and build a mythical city in the North.
The previous summer Brown had gone to Greenland “to try to buy it,” but was rebuffed, as was Trump’s emissary, Vance. (Vance, of course, is yet another Thiel protégé, and Thiel’s $15 million donation to Vance’s 2022 Senate campaign was the largest ever given to a Senate candidate. Two years later Thiel lobbied Trump to choose Vance as his running mate.) Still, despite Greenlanders’ hostility to these overtures, the Greenland saga is not over. Brown told Reuters that even after his ill-fated trip other groups had expressed their interest in establishing a new domain in Greenland, and Trump himself has not given up on his territorial ambitions, as he made clear to the Danes and other erstwhile allies at a NATO summit in early July. In August an oil company linked to Trump began setting up drilling infrastructure on the island’s east coast without permission from Greenlandic authorities.
Srinivasan’s notion of parallel institutions also extends to money and banking, education (replace Harvard with the Thiel Fellowship), and the government itself. In June 2022, shortly before the publication of The Network State, a group of tech billionaires and venture capitalists led by Garry Tan, one of the original Palantir employees, who later became the head of Y Combinator, pursued a multimillion-dollar campaign that ousted San Francisco’s progressive district attorney, Chesa Boudin, and three members of the school board. It was a bald demonstration of the power of tech money to bend politics to its will. For Srinivasan, though, it was not enough. “It may be easier to start a new city than to reform San Francisco,” he tweeted to his one million followers, during the recall campaign. On the Moment of Zen podcast, Durán writes, Srinivasan was more explicit: “The goal, he said, was to do to San Francisco what Musk had done to Twitter: Gut it, purge it, and harvest its power.”
More than Srinivasan, the most influential proponent of gutting and purging is the lachrymose, self-appointed philosopher king Curtis Yarvin, who, writing online as Mencius Moldbug, dispensed his nihilistic, burn-it-all-down militancy on a blog called Unqualified Reservations. “The other day I was tinkering around in my garage and I decided to build a new ideology,” he wrote in his first post in 2007. That ideology, which owes a debt to Ayn Rand, Carl Schmitt, Murray Rothbard, and a mash of other libertarian, fascist, and authoritarian janissaries, portrays democracy as a failed system that needs to be replaced by a national CEO, also known as, he wrote, “a dictator.” Durán points to an early essay of Yarvin’s in which he imagines a San Francisco governed by “a totalitarian corporation called Friscorp. This corporate overlord would keep its residents under constant surveillance and exercise total power over their lives. Friscorp could even execute its residents without cause.” (After the unprovoked shooting deaths of Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and Johan Guerrero by federal agents without consequences so far, this scenario feels less theoretical.) Anticipating Srinivasan’s network state concept, Yarvin also argued that people should array themselves in small city-states governed by joint-stock corporations where they would have no rights. If they were unhappy, they could vote with their feet by relocating to a different corporate entity.
As outlandish as Yarvin may seem, it would be foolish to dismiss him. Yarvin is widely credited as being the resident philosopher of what’s known as the “Thielverse,” which includes Vance, Srinivasan, Buterin, and Andreessen, among many others. (In 2013 Thiel and Andreessen Horowitz funneled more than $1 million into a company Yarvin was starting.) And as Thiel and his associates have insinuated themselves into Trump’s world, they have brought Yarvin’s ideas with them. “With the help of men like Thiel,” Durán writes, “Yarvin’s radically unhinged ideas evolved from a blogger’s musings into a serious effort to undo democracy that would be adopted by a presidential administration.”
Two days before Trump’s second inauguration, at a party at Thiel’s D.C. redoubt, the incoming vice-president, Vance, greeted Yarvin with the hail-fellow-well-met salutation “Yarvin, you reactionary fascist.” That was the same day The New York Times ran a discursive interview with Yarvin under the headline “Curtis Yarvin Says Democracy Is Done. Powerful Conservatives Are Listening.” Two of those, in addition to Vance, were Musk and Vought, who incorporated many of Yarvin’s schemes into Project 2025. “DOGE was one among many shocking triumphs for Thiel’s network in the second Trump era,” Durán writes.
For example, Yarvin had called for “a total shutdown of international relations, including security guarantees, foreign aid, and mass immigration,” all of which quickly became marquee policies of the Trump administration.
So here we are, less than halfway through a presidential administration already considered to be the most corrupt in US history. Much of that corruption has been facilitated by Silicon Valley elites who have helped Trump and his family make billions of dollars in exchange for the freedom to operate with little regulatory friction. Artificial intelligence companies, cryptocurrencies and crypto exchanges, prediction markets, and media conglomerates have all benefited. Palantir has obtained over $1 billion in government contracts from, among others, the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security, Energy, Transportation, Health and Human Services, Commerce, Agriculture, Transportation, and Veterans Affairs. Musk has cashed in prodigiously: an investigation by Senator Elizabeth Warren discovered more than a hundred ways Musk profited from his proximity to the Trump administration, including apparently getting Trump to fire the inspector general of USAID, who was investigating claims that Starlink had provided Internet services to Russia as it waged war against Ukraine. Less well-known players have also gotten in on the grift. A report from the top Democrat on the House Committee on the Judiciary, Jamie Raskin, found among other things that
the Trump Administration has intervened to halt or terminate federal investigations and enforcement actions involving multiple cryptocurrency firms that have donated to the President or invested in his companies…issued pardons and rolled back sanctions for known bad actors that have provided financial support to his ventures…[and] systematically dismantled anti-corruption and financial integrity safeguards.
Is it ideologically inconsistent that companies led by men who excoriate the federal government, profess a desire to see it dismantled, and lobby hard to skirt taxes are being enriched by our tax dollars through generous government contracts? It is not. When it comes down to it, their politics have always been motivated by the desire to amass as much money as possible; democracy is just an impediment. But cultivating the conditions for its demise takes time. A good first step is to install an executive who has no respect for the norms of democracy and prop him up with cronies who will defer to him. Is it any surprise that the largest donor in the 2026 midterm elections is Andreessen Horowitz? Again, it is not.
Money is power—that’s axiomatic. Gil Durán believes that “to create a better future, we must create a world without billionaires. We can have billionaires, or we can have democracy.” But here, I think, Durán overstates his case. He writes:
We do not allow private citizens to own nuclear weapons because such power does not belong in the hands of individuals…. A single nuke might kill hundreds of thousands of people, but the billionaires will kill millions or billions.
The problem is not that we live in a world with billionaires—it’s that we live in a world where a small coterie of billionaires with totalitarian aspirations have gotten so close to power. Durán is not wrong to repeat what have become “resistance” shibboleths—that we need to eliminate the influence of money in politics, institute real and effective regulation on artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency, and other dangerous technologies, and then, if these projects succeed, hold technofascists accountable for the damage they have done. These are all crucial.
In the short term, though, so is understanding to whom candidates vying for election in the midterms are beholden and how this support will determine their efforts to rein in hazardous technology—or not. Practicing democracy is the only way to preserve democracy. It is also a reminder that the dystopia celebrated by Thiel, Yarvin, Musk, and the tech bros in their thrall is not a given.
articles.summary:
Gil Durán’s book *The Nerd Reich* examines how a network of Silicon Valley billionaires is leveraging their wealth and political influence to dismantle democratic institutions and regulatory oversight.

### Key Points
- Tech elites, including Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, donated nearly $400 million to support Donald Trump’s reelection and influence federal policy.
- The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), led by Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy, aimed to slash federal agencies and budgets despite failing to meet its $2 trillion savings goal.
- Russell Vought, a key architect of Project 2025, has utilized the Office of Management and Budget to implement autocratic restructuring and purge federal staff.
- Silicon Valley figures are promoting "network states" and private tech cities, seeking to bypass traditional government authority through cryptocurrency and corporate-led governance.
- Companies like Palantir and various crypto ventures have secured significant government contracts and regulatory leniency through their proximity to the Trump administration.

### Why it Matters
The concentration of political power among a small group of tech oligarchs threatens to replace democratic governance with a system prioritizing corporate profit and deregulation. Understanding these alliances is essential for voters to recognize how private financial interests are actively reshaping the federal government and public policy.

articles.title: Bitcoin, copper, stocks, yields all fall; gold rises
articles.author: Omkar Godbole
articles.content:
Bitcoin  has dropped more than 2% in the past 24 hours, with some of the other major coins such as XRP (XRP), ether  and solana (SOL) sliding even further. The move looks less like a crypto-specific story and more like a broad-based exit from riskier investments.
Futures tied to copper, a closely watched barometer of global economic health, fell nearly 1%, extending Wednesday's 1.6% decline. Other growth-sensitive assets tumbled, with Asian stocks dragged lower by a rout in Korean chipmakers. Nasdaq index futures and risk-sensitive currency pairs such as Aussie dollar-Swiss franc, are down as well.
At the same time, Treasury yields are falling — meaning bond prices are rising — while gold is up 1%. The yield on the 10-year note, the benchmark borrowing rate, has dropped by eight basis points to 5.08%, extending the pullback from the recent peak of 5.36%. Treasuries and gold are often treated as haven investments.
Together, the moves point to investors reducing exposure to risk and seeking safety, with some stagflation fears mixed in.
“It feels more like a stagflationary environment where risk assets and the US dollar generally underperform, while gold outperforms,” InvestingLive analyst Giuseppe Dellamotta wrote in a market update.
Concerns the Fed will raise interest rates have been cited as one catalyst after Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected U.S. CPI report. But that concern appears to be fading.
CME fed funds futures now price in only a 29% chance of the central bank hiking its benchmark rate into the 4%–4.25% range later this month. The remaining probability is for rates to stay unchanged at 3.75%–4%. Odds briefly approached 50% after the CPI print, but quickly scaled back.
Looking ahead, Thursday’s producer price index will offer another read on how much inflation remains in the pipeline. A hot number could add fuel to the risk-off mood.
Traders will also watch the AI trade and whether it continues to unwind. Analysts at 10x Research still prefer holding bitcoin while that unwind plays out, but only as long as BTC holds above $78,000. Further, they prefer to “use ether as a hedge for BTC long positions.”
Stay alert!
Read more: For analysis of today's activity in altcoins and derivatives, see Crypto Markets Today . For a comprehensive list of events this week, see CoinDesk's "Crypto Week Ahead."
What’s trending
- BlackRock's Fink names a U.S. recession trigger, sounds alarm over $40 trillion national debt (CoinDesk): Companies are pouring so much money into the data centers that power AI that any attempt to slow it could hurt the U.S. economy, not just the stock market, said BlackRock CEO Larry Fink.
- Bitcoin mining pool once handling 2.3% of network shuts after hashrate falls 65% (CoinDesk): Crypto exchange Binance is shutting the bitcoin mining pool it launched in April 2020.
- Stocks slide as AI rout drives investors to bonds (Bloomberg): Global equities fell as a selloff in artificial intelligence gathered speed and pushed investors toward the safety of bonds.
Today’s signal
The chart shows ether’s daily price swings in candlestick format since May.
Ether is testing a dual support zone near $2,350, formed by a horizontal trendline and an ascending trendline. The horizontal line has acted as persistent support since Aug. 23, while the ascending trendline marks the bullish trend from the July lows.
A break below this confluence would signal a significant weakening of demand and could open the door to deeper losses.
