articles.title: One Windows setting helped me spot a fake PDF before I opened it
articles.author: Oluwaseun Bamisile
articles.content:
Cybercriminals are getting smarter by the day, and PDF phishing is one of the ways they try to infiltrate your PC. I almost fell victim to this a few days ago when I unknowingly downloaded a "PDF" file onto my laptop. But what saved me wasn't even the mighty Microsoft Defender. It was a simple setting in File Explorer that I've had turned on for months.
It's one of those Windows settings that's easy to overlook because it doesn't look important, and I’m pretty sure it’s disabled on your PC right now.
The "PDF" I downloaded wasn't actually a PDF
Showing file extensions revealed the real danger hiding behind a familiar icon
Last week, I received an email containing an invoice. The thing is, I was actually expecting an invoice around that time, so the message didn't seem suspicious. I downloaded the attachment without properly checking the email's contents or even verifying the sender.
I know, I know, that's poor internet security etiquette, and I take full responsibility for it. I've always advocated for protecting yourself online, but I let my guard down this time around. Thankfully, I had the File name extensions setting enabled in File Explorer, and it helped me catch something that I might otherwise have missed.
The file appeared to be named “Oluwaseun Invoice.pdf.exe”. At first, that may look like an ordinary invoice with an unnecessarily long filename. But look closely at the ending: exe. If I didn’t have the File name extensions setting turned on, it would have just appeared as “Oluwaseun Invoice.pdf”, and I might assume it’s a normal PDF file.
But the file wasn't a PDF document at all. It was a Windows executable disguised as an invoice by using a fake .pdf extension in its name. The .pdf in the middle was simply part of the filename. The final .exe extension identified the file as an executable program. And the craziest part was that the file had a PDF icon.
If I'd double-clicked the file, I could have launched a malicious program on my laptop, and this article topic might have been "How I Got Hacked by a PDF File."
Windows hides file extensions by default
Enabling one File Explorer setting makes suspicious filenames easier to spot
You would think a feature as life-saving as this would be enabled by default. But hey, it’s Windows, so it’s somehow disabled by default. At least enabling the setting is very easy.
Just open File Explorer, click View in the toolbar, hover over Show, and click File name extensions to enable the setting. If you're using Windows 10, open File Explorer, select the View tab, and check the File name extensions box.
You don't need to restart your computer, install anything, or change any security settings. Once enabled, the setting applies throughout File Explorer, making it easier to recognize the actual file types you're dealing with.
File extensions are just one part of staying safe online
Check suspicious files before opening them, and don't rely on one security feature
Turning on file extensions isn't a complete security solution. An actual malicious document can use a legitimate extension. My experience with that fake invoice was a useful reminder that even people who know a thing or two about cybersecurity can make mistakes.
So, while enabling file extensions is a great first step, there are other habits I recommend adopting. For instance, if you receive a document via email, check the actual email address and pay attention to subtle misspellings or unfamiliar domains. Even if you're expecting a document, take a moment to inspect the message and confirm that the attachment makes sense. Be very careful with files ending in .exe, .msi, .bat, .cmd, or .scr. These extensions can identify executable programs or scripts that you shouldn't run casually.
And please avoid opening suspicious files just to investigate them; I know it can be tempting, but resist the urge. If you aren’t sure about a file, delete it immediately. Also, ensure Microsoft Defender is active and up to date, as it can detect and block many malicious files before you open them. Cybersecurity is more about building small habits that make it harder for attackers to catch you off guard.
One small Windows setting could save you a big headache
I was lucky that a simple File Explorer setting helped me spot that suspicious invoice before I opened it. It was a small reminder that sometimes the most useful security features aren't the ones that make headlines.
However, enabling File name extensions won't protect you from every phishing email or malicious download. It won't replace antivirus software, careful browsing, or common sense. But it can expose a misleading filename before you make the mistake of opening it.
Because sometimes, the difference between a harmless document and a dangerous program is just a few characters at the end of a filename.
articles.summary:
Enabling the File name extensions setting in Windows File Explorer helps users identify malicious executable files disguised as legitimate PDF documents, preventing potential cyberattacks and unauthorized software installations.

### Key Points
- Windows hides file extensions by default, allowing attackers to mask malicious .exe files as harmless PDF documents.
- Users can reveal true file types by selecting "File name extensions" under the "View" menu in File Explorer.
- Malicious files often use deceptive names like "Invoice.pdf.exe" to trick users into executing harmful programs.
- Security experts recommend avoiding files ending in .exe, .msi, .bat, .cmd, or .scr unless the source is verified.
- Enabling this setting is a simple, no-cost habit that adds a critical layer of visibility to basic Windows security.

### Why it Matters
This simple configuration change provides an immediate visual defense against common phishing tactics that rely on user oversight. By exposing hidden file extensions, users can verify the true nature of attachments before opening them, significantly reducing the risk of accidental malware infection.

articles.title: A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI
articles.author: Ben Thompson
articles.content:
Good morning,
This week’s Stratechery Interview ended up not being an Interview, but rather a conversation with Hollywood super-agent Ari Emanuel. Emanuel is the Executive Chairman of WME Group, Executive Chair and CEO of TKO Group Holdings (the owner of UFC and WWE), and Founder of MARI, a live events and experiences company.
The occasion for this conversation née interview was the recent publication of Emanuel’s memoir, Roll the Calls, a reference to Emanuel’s relentless daily phone call routine; I got on Emanuel’s roll for the first time a couple of years ago, and quickly learned that when Emanuel wants something he gets it.
That’s a theme of his book, and of this interview: Emanuel decided he wanted to have a conversation and ask me some questions too, so that’s exactly what we did. We cover everything from the state of social networks, AI’s impact on Hollywood and the tech industry, and what skills might not just persist but become more valuable. We also discuss why Emanuel is making such a big bet on live, whether or not Hollywood is logical, and whether talking on the phone is the antidote to polarization.
As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.
On to the conversation:
A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI
This interview is lightly edited for clarity and content.
Topics:
The State of Social | Roll the Calls | AI and Creativity | Buying UFC | Post-AI Tech | AI and Generational Change | MARI | Hollywood Logic
The State of Social
Ari Emanuel: Can I ask you one question? Because I saw your interview. Who was it — you did it with a guy in New York.
AE: Patrick, yeah, who I love.
Yeah, I read your interview with him, it was great.
AE: I loved your point of view, and explain a little bit more to me because I love your thinking — that on a SaaS model, the only one, based on my understanding, based on your model right now, that’s got it right, OpenAI should have gone to advertising as opposed to charging, Muse has it right.
Yeah, for sure.
AE: They don’t need to charge you because they have the other revenue stream.
Right. And well, not just that, but the LLM, like, it’s actually really interesting. So when they launched Muse, they made this promise, “We won’t use your data that you use with Muse for advertising”, and no one cares. No one knows they made that promise, and no one cares, because no one cares about that stuff. And so they, in some respects, handicapped themselves by making this promise.
AE: Just like Apple, we’re not going to look at your data, major mistake when Tim [Cook] said that.
Right. But in the long run, I think it’s going to pay off, because you’re going to have this complete change in how advertising works. Right now you sort of have data on the user and you have data, broadly speaking, of what a particular product matches with and you’re matching, it’s called the two-towers approach. So you’re matching these two things together, and that’s how advertising basically works at scale, and it’s all these vector databases, all these sorts of things.
AE: Television never did it properly.
That’s right. So the way advertising is going to work in the future, and it’s already happening, is it’s going to predict what you want.
AE: Well, the funny thing, what I thought when you said that—
(laughing) I can never remember if I’ve said it before.
AE: One is, Mark is going to be able to make a ton personally and charge, he’s going to be able to use the AI to do it, and it’s going to be just more and more and more.
It’s more than that. So what you’re going to do is you’re going to get a personalized ad predictor that basically is inside your VM. They’re going to be credibly able to say it’s totally private, because it is totally private.
AE: Because it’s just directed at you.
That’s right, it’s just predicting what you want to see. Just like it’s going to be a predictor of content you want to see.
AE: Oh, I didn’t think about it that way, yeah.
The reason why there’s such massive upside is this whole agent thing — this is the real Google threat. So everyone thought when ChatGPT came out, that was a threat to Google, but the human was still in the loop. As long as the human is still in the loop, Google is okay. But all of Google Search, Amazon search—
AE: Once the human is out of the way…
Then all these search-skim ad models, which is what all these models are, they’re all bullshit models, because it’s just attacks on search.
AE: Well, are you saying the same thing about Amazon?
Yeah, 100%.
AE: I think Amazon, because of Muse — I mean, Walmart made the deal with them.
AE: Amazon’s going to have to figure out — I mean, a lot of stuff is going to go through.
Well, and the problem is that the problem with having a physical moat is that means you have a lot of capital tied up in that, which means you do have a forcing function that means you have to adjust.
AE: It’s what happens when you’re just saying that when you have a digital, not a personal, on the Amazon side, your $60 billion is in jeopardy on your advertising business. I mean, it’s a problem.
It’s a big problem, a huge problem for them. So the upside is the new products still need advertising, and things like live events, all the sorts of personalized stuff that the Internet makes possible. Like, one of the most important functions is going to be the generation of human desire, that is the post-AI economy.
AE: MARI! That’s exactly how I think about it. It’s like, you know, not only what Elon [Musk] said to me — it can’t be disintermediated.
Don’t waste it. We’re going to get to it. I get to talk now, you don’t get to talk, because I have to record this for the interview.
AE: I can’t believe we’re not recording now!
I am recording, but I didn’t say we hadn’t started yet, so maybe we can include this. We should make this more of a conversation.
AE: We can just go. This is the interview.
Okay, this is the interview, we started.
AE: Exactly how my life goes.
Okay, I’ll throw away my script here.
AE: The reason I love talking to you is this, I can’t articulate it as well as you can.
You have this massive need for the generation of human desire, and you’re going to have people like you who are creating the vessels in which to sort of collect that human desire. But that means that advertising has just been between 1% and 2% of GDP, so let’s say that holds.
AE: Oh, it’s going up more.
It has gone up with digital, yeah, it’s up to between 2% and 3% now, but historically, it’s been between 1% and 2%.
AE: I think it’s going to above that.
I think it will too. So this is the conservative estimate. Amazon advertising is impaired, and Google advertising is impaired, because there’s no more human in the loop, that advertising is going to flow to surfaces that are not impacted by AI.
AE: Facebook.
Facebook.
AE: I couldn’t think, after that conversation you had with Patrick, if there’s another group out there, and maybe it’s X? Because I think Elon’s going to do that, right? But I didn’t think of another one, another kind of digital player that could do that, except maybe Microsoft inside LinkedIn.
Which, by the way, is doing very well.
AE: Very well. Because actually that is a digital personal because people are involved.
I think social networks are only going to get more valuable over time, not less.
AE: I agree.
If anything, we’re almost at the nadir of social network value.
AE: So name the social networks in the United States. Facebook. Instagram. X. And I said LinkedIn. Did I miss one?
No, I don’t think so. So that’s the brilliant thing about Muse, it’s not only this phenomenal opportunity, it’s also a direct heat missile at Meta’s competitors, to the extent it lands, and that money’s going to flow back into Meta.
AE: And I think it actually — depending on what [Amazon CEO] Andy [Jassy] does, who’s very smart, he’s got to make a deal. Over time, he’s got to figure out that $60 billion, which is one of the biggest problems.
Here’s one thing that’s interesting, and I’m curious what you’re thinking about it. So in the long run, of course, AI is very highly deflationary but I think there’s an aspect that it is short-to-medium-term inflationary, in that ads are a subsidy to the people who are not impacted by the ads. Stuff is cheaper, Amazon is a good example — the prices Amazon charges are definitionally less than they would be absent advertising. And we know this because their advertising revenue is more than their e-commerce revenue — or their profit, I should say.
AE: And the advertising does subsidize all that.
That’s right. So if the advertising goes away and they have to charge more, that is actually inflationary to a certain extent, because prices have to go up. And I think you’re going to see this — like, for example, what’s a very easy Muse use case? Find these subscriptions that are lingering, what subscriptions do I have that I should cancel? There’s a lot of advertising businesses that are supported by people forgetting to cancel their subscription.
AE: This is the same argument I’ve been making with people. The cable business — ESPN was elevated not because so many people were watching it, there was that select group of people that had to have it, and then they could get up to $10 for it.
And everyone paid it.
AE: And once that broke with Netflix, etc., it just went away. The cable operators and cable were broken, it just fell to the ground.
Yep, and you have to pay directly for sports, so sports fans were the biggest welfare recipients in history throughout the entire cable era.
AE: And now they’re going to pay for it, but advertisers are going to pay premiums for it, because it’s a very high-end group of people that they want, on whatever platform they have.
All the video advertising, streaming advertising — particularly to your point, if they actually finally do it right. And which, by the way, Amazon is probably the furthest ahead there, generally speaking.
AE: I think [Skydance CEO] David Ellison will catch up. He hired the right CTO out of Facebook, and he’s going to build a pretty good model. The one place — would you define YouTube as a social network? It’s in between, right?
What is a social network? So is Instagram even a social network anymore? It is, to an extent. But the big shift, and the reason why TikTok sort of blindsided Meta, is TikTok is classified as a social network, but it’s not a social network at all, it’s a user-generated content network.
AE: Well, so is Reels.
That’s right, and Reels is a direct response to realizing, “Holy cow, we missed it”.
AE: And the issue is that, unlike Threads, Reels works.
There’s this famous Paul Krugman article that’s saying the Internet is not going to have any more economic impact than a fax machine.
AE: He said that?
Yeah. Maybe it was a long time ago, I wrote about 2014, he must have said it in the late ’90s, early 2000s or something. And the reason is because most people don’t have anything interesting to say and the funny thing is he was actually half right and you saw this with what happened to Facebook. As long as your content was limited to people you knew, it was fun.
AE: Everybody cared!
They came to not care, because what happened was TikTok realized, if you’re limiting what people see to only the people you know, they’re not seeing the best stuff. What the TikTok algorithm does is it basically finds the best content across the entire service, and feeds it to you, such that it’s the best content in the world — even though the percentage of good content to bad content is hilariously small. The vast majority of content sucks, but the absolute value of good content is very large, because the total amount of content is so great, even if you get a very small number on a massive denominator. And so they’re like, “We’ll just show you the best content”.
AE: And that’s what their algorithm did, they could figure that out.
That’s right, and that was Meta’s blind spot, because they killed Snapchat by leveraging their network. You already had friends — you could see a story on Instagram, and it was instantly useful to you, because you were already following people on Instagram.
AE: But why — I want to ask you a question, and this brings up Snapchat. Why hasn’t he [Snap CEO Evan Spiegel], as opposed to doing glasses, figured out he is one of the last social networks? And it’s still good. He’s got a billion users.
(laughing) There’s a lot of good questions that can be asked about Evan Spiegel‘s corporate governance, most of which are not very flattering.
AE: I mean, he is one of the last social networks, we’re talking about social networks — he’s one of the last ones, and he actually still has a great user base.
He does, and it’s still young.
AE: Very young, and they use it to talk to people.
The engagement is off the charts. If you use it, you use it all the time.
AE: And if he did it right with AI, as opposed to the glasses
I mean, this is the eternal Snapchat question. That’s why they are still such a lure to investors, despite the fact they pay out gazillions in stock-based compensation, they never seem to really make money, blindsided by Apple a few years ago, and all these sorts of things, is because it’s so clearly a tremendously valuable asset.
AE: And completely utilized by a generation.
Yeah, absolutely. So, yes, Snapchat is always a question.
AE: So now let’s get to the advertising piece on live. Because my opinion is the following, let’s just say you were right, 1% or 2%.
By the way, this is a perfect framing for this interview, where you just sort of took it over. I think we’re actually conveying, at a meta level, the experience — the Ari Emanuel experience. So anyway, continue.
AE: (laughing) Well, it’s kind of the experience, I’ve been reading your newsletter, and I just call you out of the blue, and we start talking.
Roll the Calls
Well, your book is Roll the Calls.
AE: You got one of them! I rolled you!
You did. It kind of made me scared for this interview when I was actually reading the book, I’m like, “do you actually stop for an hour and not talk on the phone?”.
AE: Yeah, because it’s an interesting conversation, I’m going to learn something.
I did remember the first time you called me.
AE: You were in Asia, weren’t you?
No, I was in Seattle the first time you called me, but I was still living in Asia. And the second time I was in Asia, I missed your call in the middle of the night. But what was striking is your assistant emailed me, I found the email asking for my phone number which says, “Ari wants to call you”. I replied, and I think my phone rang within 30 seconds, which was stunning to me.
AE: (laughing) Were you sleeping, and you had woken up and got there?
No, it was Microsoft Build, it was in May, so I was there. I think I was going to interview [Microsoft CEO] Satya [Nadella]. I was in the lounge at the Hyatt downtown getting breakfast.
AE: Oh, wow. I don’t remember what the conversation was about.
It was some Article I wrote, I don’t remember what it was.
AE: I didn’t understand it completely, and I wanted some answers.
Do you still talk on the phone as much as you did back in the ’80s?
AE: Oh my god, yeah. I don’t like this whole thing. Ron Meyer once said to me, we were talking about this — and he still reads papers, and I read papers online — and he said, “You know, if texting existed before telephones did, and then all of a sudden telephones came out, people would be calling people as opposed to texting”, because the reverse happened, texting’s cool, and people just do that. So yeah, I’d rather have a conversation.
The bandwidth is just higher.
AE: Especially for me — one, being dyslexic. Two, the misinterpretation, potentially. Larry David can write funny texting, I can’t do that.
Well, I think what’s interesting is, I mean, a lot of the book is — and you talk about this — just sort of your not giving up, I think, is a generous way to put it. Asking a million times, you mentioned the dyslexic angle, not being embarrassed, people can keep saying no — it doesn’t bother you. But I think there’s an aspect of that relentlessness combined with, in a phone call, because it’s so much higher bandwidth, you get the shape of the problem or the shape of the person much more clearly and so that pressure you’re putting on is also much more finely targeted.
AE: When I get on a phone call, like I just hung up with Marc Andreessen about something, and I didn’t understand something he was asking me, I was asking him a question. I just want the answer to that one thing. I’m not sitting here — it could be 14 calls, because I might have multiple calls, but in each situation I don’t have a long conversation. I just don’t understand something, I want an answer, I’m going to the people that I think have an answer.
That answer, for whatever my life is going on, answers some question that I want answered, to kind of continue a conversation or understand something so I can think about what we’re doing, how we’re thinking about this. This is one of the reasons I wanted to do this — because one, I love your newsletter, I read it, as you know, consistently, but I was wondering, AI, live — your point of view on it.
I have a point of view — one, that people are going to have more free time, they’re going to come to it. But also, I think there’s going to be the ability to put it on social and I think advertising in arena is going to go pretty high, because you’re concentrated and I think that’s true for both TKO and I think that time that people have now is going to be so much more precious, they’re going to have more money — we can talk about that — and it’s just like where the world’s going.
So is it “Mari”? Is that how you say it?
AE: Do you know how that name came about?
I do not.
AE: I have a Monday morning weekly call with all the executives at TKO — WWE, UFC, everybody — and we were going over, I don’t know, an advertising issue or a site fee issue and the executive goes, “Mari!”, I go, because Mark Shapiro was talking — I go, “What did you just say?”.
Oh, it was Mark and Ari.
AE: I lost my shit on him, it was hysterical, then I had shirts made with “Mari” — Mark and my face combined, it was really funny, so that’s how it came.
You mentioned, as far as the thesis, people are going to have more free time, live events are going to become more valuable.

We have our collectible business, which is Frieze, Barrett-Jackson, Collect-A-Con, which is our Pokémon experience. Then we have, like, a holiday — Winter Wonderland, our food festivals — all the stuff in that. And then we just executed against the theater business. So the West End and Broadway — we have 70 theaters in this company called ATG.
We think that is a kind of incredible — there hasn’t been one person on the live event side that exists. In the music space, it’s Live Nation and AEG. In live events, there are onesies and twosies, and so we’re trying to capture that. And what we do is, between taking things international when it’s a domestic thing — like Frieze, it was in London and New York. Now there’s two events in London, one in New York, now there’s two events in New York, one in Chicago, one in L.A., one in South Korea. And now we’re just — I think next month, we’re doing one in Abu Dhabi, and there’s other areas.
We’re going to do the same thing with Collect-A-Con on the Pokémon business, you saw how we’ve expanded when we had UFC — performance institutes and our fights all over the globe now. Then we do unbelievable sponsorship, site fees now, that’s what we do, so we’ve kind of got it down to a system of how we monetize the assets.
So what is next? Is it just acquiring more events, then, so you can plug into the system?
AE: It’s really taking our events, like Frieze, and we’re looking at different art fairs all over the place. Barrett-Jackson — can we expand it internationally? Other car auction businesses we can get into? Are there other things like Collect-A-Con — that’s Pokémon, are there other ones that we could do? And so we just look at them. When ATG came available, it’s the perfect kind of vertical that we didn’t have, that we wanted to have.
When you think about these events — but also do it like TKO and UFC and WWE — what do you think, from a business model perspective? Is it ticketing? Is it advertising? What’s the balance between those?
AE: It first starts with broadcast globally. Then from broadcast, you’re the sponsorship. Then where you take the events internationally, can you get site fees? Then you’re adding — there’s a customer that wants really high end, and will pay for really high end. And then there’s the general public, making sure their experience is incredible. And so those four or five stacks are how we think about the business, to maximize economics.
How does that align with the way you think about UFC and WWE?
AE: Those are all the things that it started. This concept started with the UFC and then we brought our sponsorship business, our site fee business to the WWE, our premium ticketing business, our ability — Mark Shapiro and myself — to make sure our broadcast deals, domestically, internationally, all of that.
For those broadcast rights business — are those, in the long run, going to be about driving subscribers or driving ads?
AE: I think for each company it’s different, but they’re all moving to an SVOD and AVOD service.
One of the things that we saw early on at the UFC, we knew that they were going to have to get to an AVOD — from a SaaS model to an advertising-based model and one of the greatest drivers there is sports, because it’s the greatest reality show. The Monday Night game — you don’t know what’s going to happen. Overtime, you think the Rams are going to win, the Bills won, and it’s the greatest model. It’s the same thing with our sports so it’s one of the great drivers and you now have four big competitors.
Do you have any concern about ending up in sort of monopsony situation where there’s not enough buyers?
AE: No. They’re all going to need it.
And there’s going to be a bunch of them?
AE: You’re now going to see what happens with Comcast and Apple. You have YouTube out there, I think all these models are going to change. One of the fastest things growing for David Ellison at Skydance is Pluto.
Right. Fox put together Roku and Tubi, which I thought was a great deal.
AE: So you’re going to have a lot of bidders. The one thing that’s great — and I think about this all the time — if the Lakers are $12.5 billion. Fantastic. Love the franchise.
Good story in your book about buying tickets.
AE: That’s a team. And that’s not the league. If a team is worth that, what are my four leagues worth? Because we have boxing, WWE.
Is that part of the allure of the UFC and WWE — you kind of get the whole thing?
AE: Yeah, running a league is different than running a team, they’re both very difficult to do. You know, they both have their personnel issues and management issues and etc. But, you know, Mark and I —
The difficulty is the moat.
AE: Mark and I run leagues. Those are hard things to do, as opposed to just a team. You’re thinking about different things, and if a team is worth that — what are the four leagues worth? I have a different conversation than the stock market is telling us right at this moment.
Is the sporting asset, given your whole model, that you are the most jealous of, Formula One?
AE: No! I think it’s an incredible sport.
Just all the things you’re talking about — the combination of the in-person events plus the rights, and all those sorts of things.
AE: I mean, think about it. First of all, I love golf, I love snooker. I mean, there’s a lot of sports that I love, that doesn’t mean that I want to be in business with them, or run them.
Hollywood Logic
Is there a world — just to go back historically a little bit — where you see streaming coming, and streaming shows up, and it’s actually this big boom, because it’s an extra window?
AE: At the time, remember, you had network syndication, so on the RSNs, you then had a cable window, it was incredible. And then all of a sudden Netflix came, you had a third window.
And is there a world where that actually persists?
AE: Well, I don’t think the syndication model — first of all, most shows are happening on streaming. You don’t get to 100 episodes, which was required.
But the reason they’re happening on streaming is because everyone decided they need to compete with Netflix. Instead, there’s a world where everyone accepts Netflix as the permanent third window, and actually makes more money all along instead of shooting themselves in the foot.
AE: That’s a logical conversation. But let me say the other side of this conversation. Do I think the network business goes to zero in cable? No, I don’t. So there is going to be a play. Remember, the original — when I was in the business, you needed to get to 100 episodes to get into syndication, now you’re doing 40 episodes.
That’s a lot these days.
AE: That’s like four seasons. So what’s the syndication window to that? It’s different. And Netflix is owning them, HBO is owning them, you’re just negotiating for the profit participants.
Is Hollywood logical?
AE: Yeah. That’s the only way I know — that you’ve been able to create over 100 years of great entertainment on the global scale, one of our great exports in the United States. Don’t you think?
Oh, for sure. Massive soft-power instrument.
AE: And I think it’s probably on the export basis — I might be wrong about this — probably our fifth or sixth most important export economically.
I write about media along with tech and Hollywood to a certain extent and my hit rate feels lower than it is, sort of, with just more tech companies and I hate the explanation that it’s because Hollywood acts more irrational.
AE: Not on every individual movie or television show. Because what do they say — if you’re batting .300 in baseball, you’re in the Hall of Fame. Same thing in Hollywood. So that’s, you know, there’s 66% — right — you’re screwing up.
Well, you mentioned David Ellison several times. Why is what he’s doing make sense?
AE: He believes if you change the tech — he believes that there’s going to be more consumption, economics for creating products is going to come down, that he’s going to be able to create unbelievable value in the SaaS model, and also take this direct-to-consumer business with the ad-based model that he has now, and also create vertical content on-site that he can kind of capture greater value than it currently exists. He’s the only one that will own his cloud, own his tech, etc. Netflix has AWS, I think Disney’s trying to change its tech right now.
Why do you need to own your own cloud?
AE: Well, I think he thinks — I think by owning that data, he’s going to get more understanding of the consumer and etc. We’ll see, that’s his point of view.
Can I ask you a question? Did you like the book?
I did. I was plowing through — no one cares about my personal schedule, but it’s been very fraught, but I was listening to it while driving, and I discovered on the plane I could listen at 3.5x speed and read at the same time, and it was unbelievable, I’ve actually never done this before.
AE: I do it all the time.
Both at the same time.
AE: I don’t look at the book. When I’m listening, I usually do a 3, 3.2x — you fly.
But if you’re listening and reading, you enter such a zone. I was flying — I flew here this morning from Chicago to L.A., I was shocked when we were landing. But it helped. I thought the book was very entertaining, I enjoyed it. How much did you write versus—
AE: You know, what we did is, when we started in 2016, [J.R. Moehringer] just kept on asking me questions. Then I answered all the questions. We met once a month, and every other week, every other month, and then he first met all my assistants.
I was going to ask you, how many assistants have you had?
AE: A lot. Some of them had kept journals, it was the craziest thing, then they met family members, friends and so he just compiled it, and then he and I went back as he was piecing it together. Then we were supposed to end when we first went public, but we didn’t go public, and then we just continued until it was 10 years.
What would you add if the book had come out a year later? What’s missing from it?
AE: I don’t know. The response has been kind of crazy from parents that have dyslexic kids, people that have dyslexia, people loving — like, re-understanding that being aggressive and rage, and taking agency for yourself, is a good thing, not a bad thing, because they’ve grown up in this place where you have to be delicate. It’s been crazy. So all in all, I’m completely happy to where it’s at right now.
Yeah. The bit about you know, you frame it as rage, but really just agency — forcing resolution.
AE: Yeah. I think that’s important to get to the end. I was having a conversation today about it. It’s like, why do I want to play this stupid game? Like — I know what you’re doing, you know that I know, let’s just have the conversation. You have to do this for this reason, I know that, just get to it already. I cannot stand this whole gray area. I can say I don’t like you, or I like you, and here’s what you did to me, and here’s how I feel about it, and go fuck yourself, and it’s ok.
Isn’t that, like, very — particularly on the West Coast — West Coast always strikes me as much more indirect, passive-aggressive.
AE: Oh you don’t think Wall Street or Silicon Valley is indirect?
No, Silicon Valley is. I think Wall Street’s much more direct.
AE: Oh you do?
I was thinking about the East Coast versus West Coast, you’re from Chicago.
AE: We’re pretty direct in Chicago.
Yeah. Is that the real secret?
AE: Maybe. I mean, it’s the only way I know how to do it, maybe that’s because I grew up with my mom and dad, and that’s what we did at our dinner table. Well, thank you.
I’ll remind you — we’ll have an ending, since we didn’t have a beginning, but thank you for coming on to Stratechery.
AE: (lauging) I appreciate it.

articles.title: Can the Shark Tank Water Bottle Really Keep Drinks Cold for 36 Hours? I Tested One to Find Out
articles.author: Joey Skladany
articles.content:
The universal push for better hydration has produced a seemingly endless supply of water bottles that promise to keep H2O cold for hours, days, even months. Admittedly, “months” is a stretch, but given recent advances in insulation technology, that milestone may not be far off.
Fresh off Stanley’s early-2020s hype, a new water bottle contender, Coldest, piqued my interest with its bold, brazen name alone. The company’s line of bottles and tumblers, which come in a range of sizes, styles and limited-edition designs, was featured on ABC’s “Shark Tank” and promises to keep beverages cold for 36 hours.
Coldest also operates out of my hometown of Naples in Florida (which I didn’t realize until I researched it), and I welcome any opportunity to support a local small business. But did it ultimately live up to its hype, the thousands of positive reviews and the praise from national media outlets?
More from CNET
The test
For comparison, I grabbed my go-to $30 Owala water bottle and filled it with equal amounts of water (three cups) and ice (one cup). This model is a different size and shape than the 46-ounce Coldest, which means the liquid and ice were more condensed in the compartment.
That said, despite the lack of error-free, controlled-environment analysis, the primary goal was to determine whether the Coldest water bottle lived up to its 36-hour promise.
The results
After only a few hours, both water bottles delivered refreshing, ice-cold agua, with Owala consistently beating Coldest by a couple of degrees. Using a meat thermometer, here is a breakdown of the reading times and temperatures across 36 hours:
After 3 Hours
- Coldest: 52°F
- Owala: 50°F
After 7 Hours
- Coldest: 54°F
- Owala: 52°F
After 15 Hours
- Coldest: 57°F
- Owala: 56°F
After 18 Hours
- Coldest: 58°F
- Owala: 57°F
After 24 Hours
- Coldest: 60°F
- Owala: 59°F
After 36 Hours
- Coldest: 63°F
- Owala: 63°F
While water certainly remained cool after the experiment concluded, it was by no means teeth-chattering cold. Though I can hardly imagine anyone waiting this long to drink a beverage, it’s still worth noting since this is a major part of Coldest’s marketing claim.
Owala’s water bottle, though smaller in volume, yielded a consistently colder liquid, likely because of its smaller surface area and greater exposure to the stainless steel interior. But after 36 hours, both bottles tied in temperature, giving Coldest a slight edge because of its significantly larger size.
The Verdict
My feelings towards Coldest were essentially neutral. While I appreciate the company’s ability to retain a cult-like following with monthly limited-edition design drops, I didn’t feel its water-cooling technology was any more superior than the models I currently own (including the Owala).
It’s clear that this was introduced to disrupt Stanley’s virality and market share, though I’m not entirely sure if I’d cough up the cash to make it part of my must-have accessory rotation. I didn’t dislike it, by any means, and applaud the founders on their early success, but even loyalty points and an affiliate program wouldn’t incentivize consistent buys, despite my obsession with staying hydrated and color-coordinating my outfits.
Those who collect water bottles like Pokémon will certainly think otherwise, as the impressive range of designs can be exciting. They are one-of-a-kind, often glow in the dark, and reflect current seasons and holidays, which is undeniably adorable. If that’s your thing, then great. But if your main concern is quenching thirst, you’re likely thinking less about style and more about substance, so any popular drinking vessel will do.

articles.title: Jury finds Arm guilty in licensing breach, Qualcomm awarded just $2 in total
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- A Delaware jury sided with Qualcomm this week, finding Arm guilty of breaching a licensing agreement and "interfering" with business relations.
- Qualcomm was awarded $1 in damages for each offense, but the shouting will continue: the companies will likely find themselves in court over royalty payments.
- This started over Qualcomm's allegations that Arm "violated its contract" after its 2021 acquisition of Nuvia.
Qualcomm's court case with Arm was settled this week, and the former came out the victor ... in a way.
Reuters reported this week that a recent court case between Qualcomm and Arm over an alleged licensing breach has been settled. A Delaware jury found Arm guilty of the breach and of "interfering" with Qualcomm's business relationships, and as a result, Qualcomm was awarded $2 in damages — $1 for each offense.
While the jury officially sided with Qualcomm, Arm saw it differently. In a statement, the company said "the jury’s verdict confirms that Arm operated in good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only two dollars confirms the merit of Arm’s arguments in the case."
This likely won't be the end of Qualcomm and Arm's court dates. According to Reuters, Qualcomm has more to bring up, which it will likely do in court with Judge Maryellen Noreika. Since Arm neglected its responsibilities of providing the necessary tools for its chips, Judge Noreika could rule that Qualcomm can "stop paying royalties to Arm for five years." This is something Qualcomm has been after since this dispute began.
So far, Arm is against such a ruling. It remains to be seen what will happen.
Qualcomm's allegations
Qualcomm and Arm's court case began in early October. The former wants to freeze royalty payments for up to five years, a ruling Judge Noreika will have to decide in the future. But it all started after Qualcomm’s 2021 acquisition of the chip startup Nuvia. As stated before, Qualcomm alleged Arm "violated its contract" by withholding its chip-testing tools.
Beyond this were Qualcomm's business relationships. The company claimed Arm "leaked its threat to end a key license in 2024." This reportedly hurt Qualcomm's potential chip deal with Meta that year. Qualcomm said this leak dropped $170 million off its deal with Meta. Arm denied that it was linked to any of this. Instead, Meta's change of heart from VR headsets to AI glasses was the real reason, the company claimed.

There's still a concern that the fallout of these cases could impact future phone prices. Price negotiations and control over CPU technology could be hit the hardest.

### Key Points
- A jury found Arm guilty of breaching its technology license agreement and interfering with Qualcomm’s business relations.
- Qualcomm was awarded nominal damages of $1 for each of the two offenses cited in the verdict.
- The dispute originated from Qualcomm’s 2021 acquisition of Nuvia and allegations that Arm withheld essential chip-testing tools.

### Why it Matters

The outcome of future court rulings could fundamentally alter how chip designers and manufacturers negotiate licensing fees, potentially impacting the cost and development of future mobile hardware.

articles.title: Colleges Are Automating Admissions, but Their Most Time-Consuming Work Is Still Manual — And Costly
articles.author: Ashish Fernando
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Colleges have automated the easy work (CRM, communication) while the hardest, most labor-intensive work (transcript evaluation, fraud checks) stays manual.
- Enrollment growth targets are outpacing the processing capacity needed to handle more applications.
- Admissions leaders want AI to extend staff capacity, not replace human judgment on consequential decisions.u003cbru003e
Higher education has invested in digital transformation for years. Colleges have adopted student information systems, customer relationship management platforms, online application portals and increasingly sophisticated communication tools. Yet many admissions teams still face significant operational challenges.
EDMO’s The State of Automation in Admissions Report 2026 offers a closer look at that contradiction. Our online survey of 40 higher education leaders at U.S. colleges and universities examined enrollment priorities, automation maturity, processing workloads, artificial intelligence and student communication.
The findings reveal an interesting divide. While 80% of respondents reported automating CRM and data synchronization and 75% reported automating student communication, only 12.5% reported automating transcript and credit evaluation. Identity and fraud checks were automated by just 17.5%.
These findings suggest that institutions have made considerable progress in automating routine administrative activities. However, some of the processes that require the most staff effort remain largely manual.
For business leaders beyond higher education, the distinction is important: introducing automation is not the same as removing the bottlenecks that constrain an organization.
The most difficult work is often the least automated
Among surveyed leaders, 70% identified staffing and workload as a major admissions challenge. Data silos and system integration followed at 50%, while 47.5% cited transcript and credit evaluation.
These pressures become easier to understand when looking at the processes that remain manual. Nearly two-thirds of respondents identified transcript and credit evaluation as largely manual. Document intake and indexing, along with identity and fraud checks, were each cited by 52.5%.
International transcripts present an additional challenge. Some 72.5% of respondents identified them among the most difficult documents to process, reflecting the complexity of evaluating different educational systems, grading scales and academic records.
The broader lesson is that organizations should examine where work becomes complicated, not simply where it is easiest to deploy technology.
For an admissions office, that may mean understanding how long a transcript waits for evaluation, how many times an incomplete document moves between teams and how frequently staff must correct or re-enter information.
Automating these processes requires more than digitizing documents. It requires workflows capable of managing inconsistent information, handling exceptions and connecting the systems involved.
Enrollment ambitions are moving faster than operational readiness
The survey also reveals a tension between institutional priorities and operational capacity.
Growing enrollment and reaching new markets was ranked the highest priority by 67.5% of respondents. Increasing yield and conversion emerged as the next major priority, with 55% assigning it second place.
Yet 47.5% rated their institution’s admissions automation maturity at three out of five. Budget constraints were cited as a barrier by 65%, followed closely by change management and staff readiness at 62.5%. Integration complexity affected 45%.
This combination creates a planning challenge. An institution may successfully increase applications but discover that its evaluation, verification and decision workflows cannot expand at the same pace.
That makes operational capacity an important part of any enrollment strategy.
Before committing to higher application targets, institutions should examine their processing capacity, identify their most time-consuming activities and assess whether existing systems can support additional volume.
Technology investments also need to account for staff readiness. A promising AI application offers limited practical value if it cannot integrate with existing systems or if employees lack the training and confidence to use it effectively.
Student communication is increasingly a capacity issue
Admissions operations are not limited to processing documents and making decisions. Institutions must also respond to students who need clarification about application requirements, financial aid, transfer credits and admission status.
The survey found that 47.5% of respondents reported average inquiry response times of two to 24 hours. Another 15% reported response times exceeding 24 hours.
Meanwhile, 72.5% said their institutions did not provide around-the-clock applicant support. Nearly half reported that 20–40% of student inquiries required staff intervention.
These findings raise an important question: how much time should admissions professionals spend answering repetitive questions when they also manage complex evaluations and consequential decisions?
Automated communication can handle routine requests, provide application updates and make information available outside traditional working hours. However, institutions must still establish clear escalation paths for questions that require personal assistance or professional judgment.
The objective should be to improve access to information while ensuring staff remain available for interactions where their expertise is essential.
Fraud concerns make human oversight essential
Growing fraud concerns add another dimension to admissions automation.
Within the surveyed group, 65% reported an increase in application or financial-aid fraud during the preceding two years. That included 40% who reported a significant increase and 25% who reported a somewhat increased level.
At the same time, 52.5% relied on manual identity verification, while only 15% reported using automated identity verification.
Institutions therefore face two competing pressures: processing applications more efficiently while maintaining reliable verification and appropriate safeguards.
The findings also suggest that admissions leaders are not looking to remove humans from these processes. When asked about the importance of human review of AI outcomes, 65% assigned a rating of four or five on a five-point scale.
This points toward a model in which technology assists with extracting information, identifying inconsistencies, routing exceptions and supporting administrative decisions, while people remain responsible for reviewing consequential outcomes.
For institutions introducing AI, oversight should be part of the original workflow design rather than an additional requirement introduced after deployment.
The real measure of automation is capacity
The most useful conclusion from this research is not that colleges need more AI. It is that institutions need a clearer understanding of where automation can meaningfully improve their operations.
Student communication and data synchronization are important, but automating these activities alone does not resolve the difficulties involved in evaluating transcripts, verifying applicant identities or managing complex applications.
Institutions should begin by identifying the work that consumes the most staff time, examining how information moves between systems and determining which activities require professional judgment.
They should then measure automation against operational outcomes: processing times, staff hours, exception rates, response capacity and the quality of human review.
For leaders in any industry, the principle is similar. The value of automation should not be judged simply by the number of tasks completed without human involvement. Its greater value lies in creating the capacity for people to focus on the work that matters most.
Key Takeaways
- Colleges have automated the easy work (CRM, communication) while the hardest, most labor-intensive work (transcript evaluation, fraud checks) stays manual.
- Enrollment growth targets are outpacing the processing capacity needed to handle more applications.
- Admissions leaders want AI to extend staff capacity, not replace human judgment on consequential decisions.u003cbru003e

The State of Automation in Admissions Report 2026 reveals that U.S. colleges struggle to scale enrollment because labor-intensive tasks like transcript evaluation remain largely manual despite digital investments.

### Key Points
- While 80% of institutions automated CRM systems, only 12.5% have automated transcript and credit evaluations.
- Nearly 65% of surveyed leaders reported an increase in application or financial aid fraud over the last two years.
- Approximately 70% of admissions leaders identified staffing and heavy workloads as their primary operational challenges.

### Why it Matters
Many institutions are prioritizing enrollment growth without first addressing the operational bottlenecks that prevent efficient application processing. By failing to automate complex tasks, colleges risk overwhelming their staff and hindering their ability to manage increased student volume effectively.
