articles.title: Meta Ships Muse Wonder, Jev Raises $870M 24 Days After Launch, and Anthropic Cuts Haiku 90%: The Top Takeaways From This Week’s 20VC x SaaStr
articles.author: Jason Lemkin
articles.content:
Pro rata goes to Delaware, Nvidia circles Reflection, a record 42 decacorns, and why the B2B apocalypse never ended for anyone under $1B in ARR
A nuclear startup took its earliest institutional backer to court over a spring-back clause. Meta put its first model at the frontier. A 20-person team raised $870 million less than a month after launching. Anthropic cut Haiku pricing by 90%. And Bending Spoons started the Airtable layoffs that were obvious from the day the deal was announced in August. Harry Stebbings, Rory O’Driscoll and I covered all of it this week.
Pro rata goes to Delaware, Nvidia circles Reflection, a record 42 decacorns, and why the B2B apocalypse never ended for anyone under $1B in ARR
Meta is back at the frontier, a 20-person team raised $870 million less than a month after launch, and Anthropic made its small model 90% cheaper. A nuclear startup also sued its own early investor, and Bending Spoons started cutting at Airtable. Harry Stebbings, Rory O’Driscoll and I went through all of it.
#1. Valar Atomics Sued Day One Ventures Over Pro Rata in Its $1B Series B
Valar is raising roughly $1B at about $6B, led by Sequoia. CEO Isaiah Taylor says Valar asked major investors to take zero allocation so a spring-back pro rata clause wouldn’t trigger, and everyone agreed except Day One, which put $1M into the seed and $15M into the A and owns under 5%. Day One GP Masha Bucher says it offered to give up most of its allocation, and Valar demanded it give up its rights in every future round. Valar then sued in Delaware for a declaratory judgment. Day One did not sue Valar, despite what X said.
Jason’s read: Everyone’s a little wrong. The big funds put “everyone waives” in every term sheet, and letting one existing investor in as a “strategic” was going to annoy Day One. But once the founder decides, you raise it once and let it go. It’s not your company and it’s not your cap table.
I learned this the hard way. I was the only investor in a company for years, then got cut to zero in a round where Harry got an allocation. I said something, and it bent the relationship with the founder. Harry didn’t know until this episode.
Rory’s read: Ask what you’d actually win. Day One’s 5% is already worth around $300M. They’re fighting to put maybe $10M to $15M more in at $6B. “Both people can be intellectually wrong but pragmatically right.”
Harry’s read: The tide is turning on pro rata. Neo says it stopped taking pro rata rights this year and cited this exact dispute. The pushback: Neo doesn’t need follow-on, and the megafunds asking seed investors to waive never waive their own.
#2. Meta Shipped Muse Wonder, Its First Frontier Model
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, scoring comparably to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra on Meta’s own tests. Wonder costs $4/$20 per million tokens on the API. Wonder Full, the one that earned the frontier scores, is only available inside Muse Code.
Jason’s read: I can’t put the headline model in my own app, so for builders it’s mostly a performative eval. The bigger story is the Muse consumer app. There’s a real chance Meta has a monster AI product on its hands.
Rory’s read: Meta was at the front on open weights, faded, and is back near the front with closed models. “If we’re going to spend $100 billion, we at least be able to charge for the damn thing.”
Jason on the people: Zuck’s had a lonely stretch. Finding a true right hand is hard. Alexandr Wang may turn out to be the WhatsApp of acqui-hires.
#3. Nvidia Is in Talks to Buy or Deepen Its Stake in Reflection AI
The FT reported Nvidia is in early talks to acquire Reflection or invest more, possibly as an acqui-hire to avoid regulatory review. Nvidia has already invested $800M, and Reflection last raised at a $25B pre-money. Harry put the rumored price around $30B. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9B in September.
Rory’s read: Nvidia wants more of the AI dollar going to chips and less to model companies, so it loves open models. “We’re the best of friends… but we’re watching you closely.” On Reflection’s board, he’d take the bid.
Jason’s read: I’ve been on the other side of this. Saying no is scary when Nvidia tells you, smiling, it’ll fund your competitor instead. Give it 18 months and Nvidia’s open model could be the default.
#4. Jev Maker TypeSafe Raised $870M at $7.5B, 24 Days After Launch
a16z led an $870M Series A at $7.5B, with Sequoia and DCVC. Jev launched September 15. It returns calibrated decisions instead of text, the company has about 20 employees, and it says a third of the Fortune 500 use it.
I did a parody of the megafund investment committee: buy every share, block the pro rata, mark it to $15B, tell the LPs we’re geniuses. Rory: “accurate as hell.”
Jason’s actual read: I use Jev in production. It’s fast, cheap and right maybe 70% to 80% of the time on carefully prompted decisions. If a team doing nothing else gets it to very high accuracy, it wins, and I doubt Cloudflare or Amazon keep investing in a niche line item. Cautiously bullish.
Rory’s read: $200B of frontier inference, 20% decision workloads, prices down 80%, Jev takes half. That’s a $4B revenue company worth about $50B, and he thinks each of those assumptions is reasonable. Competition is the risk.
Harry’s read: Every deal at these prices ends with “worst case, a great acquirer buys it.” I hear it every single time. Not everything gets bought.
#5. A Record 42 Decacorns So Far in 2026
PitchBook counts 42 new decacorns globally in 2026, with three months left. The previous record was 34 in 2021.
Rory’s read: Public markets have produced about 20 tech decacorns a decade for five decades. This year produced 42 in ten months. Either this is the most transformative event since the Industrial Revolution, “or we’re getting a wee bit ahead of ourselves.”
Jason’s read: We’re all betting it’s real. A big fund deploying in 12 months needs four $25B-plus exits, and there may only be about 70 of those ever. Andreessen was mocked for overpaying for winners and was right.
#6. Isomorphic Labs Is in Talks at a $40B to $50B Valuation
The DeepMind drug-discovery spinout is in early talks at $40B or more, five months after a $2.1B Series B led by Thrive.
Jason’s read: Generational talent gets generational pricing. I only recently bought AI drug discovery. GLP-1 data changed my mind. Getting the next one out five years faster is a bigger market than inference.
Rory’s read: This is AI that makes money from discovery, not replacing labor. You want royalties on a $200B drug. The hard part is capturing value before phase one, two and three.
#7. Mecka Raised a $60M Series B From Sequoia for Robotics Training Data
Mecka pays people to wear sensors doing everyday tasks and sells the data to humanoid trainers. It reported $100M-plus in run-rate revenue in June and expects $300M by year end, with 40 to 60 people.
Rory’s read: Same pattern as LLM data vendors, with one gap: the robots aren’t deployed yet. One logistics company counted 42 humanoid PoCs and zero deployments.
Jason’s read: I’d rather own this than any robot maker. One founder I met did $30M in 60 days in niche training data and is turning away $270M of demand.
Rory’s pushback: That’s like picking Scale over Anthropic. If you can pick the winner, pick the winner.
#8. Anthropic Cut Haiku Pricing by 90% With Haiku 5.5
Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens for prompts under 100K, down from $1/$5. Anthropic says 90% of prior Haiku requests fall in that tier.
Jason’s read: This is the first thing in AI that’s actually been deflationary for me. Haiku 5.5 is nearly Sonnet for a lot of use cases at a tenth the price. Sonnet 5.5 is twice as fast in my testing. Evals don’t talk enough about speed. No more excuses at board meetings.
Rory’s read: Cut price 90% and “we’ll use more” doesn’t cut it. You need 10x more usage or revenue falls.
I think we’ll get the 10x. You stop sampling and run it on every row of the database.
#9. Bending Spoons Is Laying Off a “Large Part” of Airtable
Bending Spoons bought Airtable in August for $1.285B in enterprise value. This week it said a large part of the team is being laid off. Evernote and Vimeo went the same way.
Jason’s read: Nobody talked about the jobs when the deal was announced. If you sell to Bending Spoons, you know your team is gone. I wouldn’t do it with a cash-flow positive company and hundreds of millions in the bank.
Rory’s read: Legally, the board’s job is shareholder value. And sometimes resolution is better for employees than a two-year death march. Take the deal, but negotiate employee terms up front.
Jason on Cloudflare: Cloudflare was crushing it and still cut 20% in a day because it was too slow. It reaccelerated. Netflix at 5% and HubSpot at 7% are too small.
#10. Bumble Is Going Private for $1.3B
Ithaca Holdings, led by Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, is paying $6.05 a share, a 138% premium. Bumble was worth about $14B at its 2021 IPO.
Rory’s read: Half of couples meet on apps, and the category is worth a few billion. VCs have always hated the churn.
Jason’s read: Having built an AI matching product, I see a bull case. Use the data to get people five great dates instead of 20 bad ones, then charge 5x more.
Harry’s read: AI avatars that date for you. Rory: “a wonderfully antisocial way to date.”
#11. The B2B Apocalypse Only Ended for Companies Over $1B in Revenue
Software stocks bottomed in March and April. By Jason’s count, the Nasdaq is up about 22% this year, his SaaS AI index about 28%, and the WisdomTree cloud index about 25%.
Jason’s read: It only passed for companies with massive scale. Everyone else is worse off than in March, because no one wants to buy software. A $500M ARR IPO may not be safe anymore. You might need $1.5B to $2B.
Harry’s read: Pre-AI companies can still get a good outcome if they go AI-first. 20VC portfolio company TechWolf, an HR software company that rebuilt itself around AI, just agreed to sell to SAP in what it says is the largest venture-backed software acquisition in Belgian history.
Rory’s read: It’s a mature, consolidating industry now. There are 200 to 300 midsize companies and big tech buys maybe 10 a year. Most will stay midsize.
Quotable Moments
Jason Lemkin
“You just got to get in line and move on. It’s not your company. It is not your cap table.”
“These are really the first thing that’s actually been deflationary with AI. No matter how much we talk about token prices falling, we’ve been consuming so many more tokens, we’re not getting the benefit of it.”
“Everyone without massive scale is living a worse apocalypse than in March or April, because no one wants to buy software. Everyone’s breathing a sigh of relief. I don’t think we should be.”
Rory O’Driscoll
“Both people can be intellectually wrong but pragmatically right.”
“Either this is the most economically transformative event since the Industrial Revolution, or we’re getting a wee bit ahead of ourselves.”
“When you cut prices by 90%, ‘we’re going to use more’ doesn’t cut it. We’ve got to use 10 times more.”
Harry Stebbings
“I love the salaciousness of this market. I remember when it was quite boring.”
“What worries me in every justification for a lot of these prices is, ‘the downside protection is that it’ll just get bought by a great acquirer.’ I just hear this every single time.”
“AI avatars that represent you, and then you can go out and meet a hundred different people without actually spending any time meeting anyone.”
articles.summary:
The tech industry faces a wave of rapid AI developments, including massive funding rounds, significant pricing shifts, and ongoing corporate restructuring across the software and robotics sectors.

### Key Points
- Jev maker TypeSafe raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation just 24 days after its launch.
- Anthropic reduced the price of its Haiku 5.5 model by 90% to drive higher enterprise adoption.
- Meta released its first frontier-level AI model, Muse Wonder, while Nvidia explores a potential acquisition of Reflection AI.
- A record 42 companies have reached decacorn status in 2026, surpassing the previous 2021 record of 34.
- Bending Spoons initiated significant layoffs at Airtable following its $1.285 billion acquisition of the company in August.
- Valar Atomics has filed a lawsuit against early investor Day One Ventures regarding a disputed pro rata investment clause.

### Why it Matters
The current market environment highlights a stark divide where only the largest, AI-integrated firms are thriving while smaller B2B software companies continue to struggle with stagnant demand. This trend suggests a period of intense industry consolidation where massive capital inflows are increasingly concentrated in a few high-growth, frontier-AI ventures.

articles.title: Help TDS Linked to Hotejka as 20,000+ Cloudflare Pages Domains Host Tech Support Scams
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
A long-running Traffic Distribution System (TDS) known as Help TDS to a Russian-language affiliate program called Hotejka, which appears to be a rebrand of a traffic monetization operation dubbed ROI777.
Help TDS is assessed to be active since at least 2017, offering PHP code templates to partners and affiliates that are installed into compromised websites with an aim to direct unsuspecting users to tech support scams. These scams make use of full-screen browser manipulation and exit prevention techniques to serve bogus Microsoft Windows security alert screens instructing victims to contact a Windows Support number to address the problem.
"Help TDS delivers tech support scams (TSSs) that direct users to call centers, where social engineering is used to convince them to install remote desktop tools," Infoblox said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It's not simple credit card fraud: it's remote access, living-off-the-land malware operations. Once in, the threat actor can exploit the victim time and again."
Help TDS's evolution was documented by GoDaddy in August 2025, highlighting the threat actor's use of a malicious WordPress plugin named "woocommerce_inputs" on thousands of websites to steal WordPress user credentials and facilitate the malicious redirections by fetching the URLs from its command-and-control (C2) servers. The plugin, or alternatively a custom HTML block, is injected into the sites by Hotejka's affiliates.
Historical tracking of malicious redirect chains has also uncovered that Help TDS has routinely handed off traffic directly to VexTrio Viper, a cybercrime operator that runs an affiliate program to enable scams, riskware, spyware, adware, and pornographic content.
The latest findings connect the TDS to Hotejka, which, in turn, is suspected to be a successor to ROI777, an entity that was exposed by Guardicore Labs (now part of Akamai) in June 2018 in connection with a traffic manipulation and cryptocurrency mining campaign codenamed Operation Prowli.
The activity involved the compromise of vulnerable servers to deploy a malware named r2r2 and then leverage them to mine cryptocurrency. In tandem, WordPress sites and servers running other content management systems (CMS) were exploited for traffic monetization fraud.
"Traffic monetizers, such as ROI777, buy traffic from 'website operators' such as the Prowli attackers and redirect it to domains on demand," Guardicore Labs noted at the time. "Website 'operators' earn money per traffic sent through roi777. The destination domains frequently host different scams, such as fake services, malicious browser extensions and more."
The rebrand is believed to be driven by the leak of data obtained from ROI777's servers in March 2018, around when it was operating Disposable TDS, a precursor to Help TDS. The published details included Telegram identities of its users and specifics about multiple campaigns.
The connection between Hotejka and ROI77 doesn't end there, for GoDaddy also found that "roi777[.]com" was one of the historical C2 domains used between 2018 and 2020 to fetch the redirect domains.
"[Hotejka's] affiliates range from spam operators to website compromisers," Infoblox said. "Potential victims are redirected into the TDS from these affiliates via special URLs provided by Hotejka. The TDS then evaluates the user via browser fingerprinting and location to determine the course of action."
A TDS functions akin to a relay, intercepting internet traffic from compromised websites, malicious ads, social media posts, or SEO spam, analyzing the visitor, filter traffic based on predefined criteria (e.g., geographic location, device metadata, IP reputation, and headless browsers), and dynamically route them to scams, browser lockers, or malware drops.
"Help TDS and its precursors are the routing decision infrastructure for a small affiliate program," Infoblox explained. "Other threat actors, for example ones who have compromised websites, send potential victim traffic to the TDS through specially crafted URLs."
The TDS is believed to be implemented on Keitaro, an advertising performance tracking platform that's known to be abused by various threat actors. Some of the initial Help TDS lures prompt users of an impending Windows update, followed by a warning that the machine has been disabled by Microsoft, tells them not to restart the computer, and that a "computer lock" has been put in place to block illegal activity.
The scareware prompt is designed to persuade the victim to contact the Microsoft Technical Support team. Should the victim make the phone call, the threat actor on the other end instructs them to download and install a free remote desktop tool like Ultraviewer to gain complete control of the infected machine.
The fingerprinting step determines whether to route the user to either the tech support scam or to another affiliate marketing platform, which then evaluates the device again and resells the traffic. These pathways lead to scam landing pages with fake CAPTCHA checks to enroll the victim's browser to push-notification spam.
"Historical DNS records, loyal use of other affiliate advertising platforms over the years, and consistent command-and-control (C2) mechanisms give us a high degree of confidence that ROI777 and Hotejka are one and the same," Infoblox said.
Messages posted by Hotejka on their Telegram channel (@hotejka_hot) demonstrate their criminal intent by advertising forced browser extension installations and tech support landing pages that are "very difficult to exit." In one post dated July 17, 2026, the operator claimed a "small call center in Germany will handle 50-100 calls per day."
Since April 2026, the scams are run on free Cloudflare Pages sites (*.pages[.]dev), with the threat actor creating roughly 300 disposable pages per day. Over 20,000 such domains have been detected since then. In recent years, Hotejka has also been observed using different aliases on forums like CrackingX, seeking traffic from email spam and access to WordPress admin panels for prices starting at $100.
In all, about 20 different affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay, send traffic to Help TDS. These operations are known to heavily target WordPress sites to redirect victims to scams and malware.
"Hotejka/ROI777 has been loyal to the two affiliate platforms since 2017, and we believe that loyalty has paid handsomely," Infoblox said. "Using DNS volumes observed over the past 8 years, our ability to use affiliate IDs to track traffic over time, and commonly cited payout figures for affiliate advertising in general, we suspect that the two European programs have paid them at least a few million dollars (USD)."
articles.summary:
The long-running Help Traffic Distribution System, linked to the Hotejka affiliate program, continues to facilitate widespread tech support scams by redirecting users from compromised websites to fraudulent call centers.

### Key Points
- Help TDS has been active since 2017 and is identified as a rebranded successor to the ROI777 operation.
- The system uses malicious WordPress plugins and custom HTML blocks to redirect traffic from compromised sites to fake Microsoft security alerts.
- Victims are coerced into installing remote desktop tools, allowing attackers to gain persistent access to their devices for further exploitation.
- Hotejka utilizes Cloudflare Pages to host thousands of disposable scam domains, generating approximately 300 new landing pages daily.
- The operation coordinates with various affiliates, including Balada Injector and Detour Dog, to monetize traffic through scams and malware distribution.
- Researchers estimate the criminal enterprise has generated millions of dollars in illicit revenue over the past eight years.

### Why it Matters
This operation highlights the sophisticated infrastructure behind modern cybercrime, where specialized routing systems allow diverse threat actors to monetize compromised web traffic at scale. By evolving through rebrands and leveraging legitimate platforms, these groups maintain long-term profitability while posing a persistent risk of remote access and financial fraud to unsuspecting users.

articles.title: Review roundup: RTX Spark's biggest surprise isn't performance
articles.author: sean.endicott@futurenet.com (Sean Endicott) , Sean Endicott
articles.content:
NVIDIA's RTX Spark is almost here. Laptops powered by the chip launch on October 16, 2026, but reviews of the chip are already out.
Reviews of the first wave of RTX Spark laptops work a bit differently than some other product launches. Today, those who were given access to RTX Spark laptops can share their experience with the chip itself, but thoughts on specific RTX Spark laptops cannot be shared until October 16, 2026.
While that is different than what we normally see, it's not that surprising. RTX Spark is not just a new chip akin to a new processor from AMD, Intel, or Qualcomm. It is a new platform for NVIDIA, a major addition to Windows on Arm computing, and the mark of a new silicon partner for Windows.
Note that reviewers of the RTX Spark were limited to sharing details about the performance and benchmarks of the processor. Dedicated GPU performance varies based on the laptop it's paired with, so some reviewer experiences may differ depending on the hardware used to test RTX Spark.
RTX Spark: Reviews
- Windows Central: "The RTX Spark GPU is very performant and is capable of pretty much handling anything you'd want to throw at it on a mobile workstation. Where it really shines, however, is running local AI models directly on it. It's the reason NVIDIA built this platform to begin with, and it does this very well."
- Tom's Hardware: "Still, for a first-generation mobile platform that joins complex silicon IP from multiple design teams onto one chip and relies on several OEM partners to bring it to life in highly integrated notebook form factors, the maturity of the RTX Spark platform is an impressive achievement. (Take it from someone who has seen a couple of rough product launches from the inside.)"
- Tom's Guide: "Judging RTX Spark purely by its single-core CPU speeds is like judging a Ferrari by its cup holders. And after a week of stress-testing the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with Spark — running every synthetic and real-world test we can throw at it — it's clear that this is so much more."
- HotHardware: "In its most potent form, which is what we’ve tested here, the RTX Spark N1X is a powerful SoC that offers competitive multi-threaded CPU performance versus today’s top mobile platforms, with class-leading GPU performance. The RTX Spark N1X’s AI performance and capabilities are also unmatched, not only because of the powerful hardware on tap and unified memory architecture, but because NVIDIA’s AI software stack is so pervasive and mature."
- Lowyat: "For NVIDIA? They basically took multiple pages out of Qualcomm’s book of trial and errors, added their gaming DNA, made damn sure that the majority of compatibility issues between the x86 and ARM architectures were resolved, and what you have is something I’d never thought I’d see: playing AAA titles on an SoC, along with all the accoutrements that comes with an NVIDIA chipset."
NVIDIA RTX Spark shows promise, but you have to understand who it is for
Early impressions of RTX Spark are largely positive. Across multiple reviews, experts praised the processor's strong GPU performance, AI capabilities, and surprisingly polished first-generation experience.
At the same time, several reviewers cautioned against viewing RTX Spark through the lens of traditional gaming benchmarks, reminding readers that the platform is designed for AI workloads, creators, and developers.
The RTX Spark is not meant to power gaming laptops. It is aimed at developers and high-end creators. The processor is especially focused on local AI performance, an area many expect to be the next major shift in personal computing.
That being said, the RTX Spark is capable of gaming. It may show the future of Windows on Arm gaming, but that's yet to be seen. Over the coming weeks I am sure we will see countless reviewers test games on RTX Spark laptops. I think they'll be surprised by how well the processor does, but gaming-focused reviews still won't be the best way to judge those PCs.
The first wave of RTX Spark laptops are already available for preorder and hit shelves tomorrow. Our Cale Hunt rounded up all the RTX Spark laptops you can buy, which you can also find below.
Built around the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform with an N1X CPU, RTX GPU, and up to 128GB of unified memory, the Surface Laptop Ultra hits new performance heights for power users. It's all contained in a gorgeous chassis with a mini-LED display and tons of ports. Prices start at $2,599.99, and units will begin shipping on October 16, 2026.
The new ASUS ProArt P14 and P16 duo gives users more size options while retaining the same great RTX Spark performance. The P14 is the lightest ProArt laptop ever, while the P16 is the way to go for a larger OLED display. Prices start at $2,599.99 for the P14 and $2,799.99 for the P16. They're expected to begin shipping on October 16, 2026.
Dell's new XPS 16 with RTX Spark features a 3.2K OLED display, lattice-free keyboard, and the usual premium XPS styling. Prices start at $3,799.99 and units are expected to begin shipping on October 16, 2026.
The OmniBook X 14 is the smaller of the two new PCs, but it features the same RTX Spark options for maximum performance. Models start at $2,999.99 and are expected to ship beginning November 4, 2026.
The larger of the two new HP RTX Spark laptops delivers a gorgeous 16-inch OLED display with 3K resolution and, of course, your choice of RTX Spark chips. Prices start at $3,199.99, and shipments are expected to begin on November 4, 2026.
Lenovo's Yoga 9n should be the right choice for those who value a versatile convertible design and premium build quality. Prices start at $3,099.99, and models are expected to begin shipping on October 16, 2026.
MSI's Prestige N16 Flip AI+ is another versatile convertible featuring the RTX Spark platform and a Tandem OLED display. It appears that preorders might kick off on October 8 for this laptop, with prices starting at $3,299.99.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Sean Endicott is a News Writer at Windows Central, where he covers Windows 11, Surface hardware, Microsoft 365, AI, apps, and the broader PC ecosystem. Since joining the site in 2017, he has written well over a thousand articles across the Microsoft landscape, covering breaking news, analysis, and feature reporting.
He writes Windows Wrap, a weekly column covering the biggest stories in Windows and the PC industry, and what they mean for the platform going forward.
Before joining Windows Central full-time, Sean worked in journalism and media production after earning a First Class degree in Broadcast Journalism from Nottingham Trent University. Outside of tech, he is an award-winning American football coach based in Nottingham, England, and was named BAFCA Youth Coach of the Year in 2024.

articles.title: Why We're Banning AI
articles.author: Nathan J. Robinson
articles.content:
Why We’re Banning AI
We urgently need to protect human thought and creativity. Our magazine is committing itself to remaining handmade. Ensure every publication you support does the same.
Iam proud to say that as part of our new union contract, Current Affairs recently adopted one of the strictest anti-AI policies in the publishing industry. No text that is AI-generated may be published in our magazine. No AI-generated art may be used as a Current Affairs illustration. When you read Current Affairs, you are going to be reading the thoughts of a human, and seeing the results of human artistry.
We’re adopting this policy because we want to directly challenge the slopification of media. Newsrooms across the country are rushing to embrace AI and replace actual writers, public opinion be damned. The CEO of Business Insider, for instance, has said his publication is “all in on AI” (which is becoming an annoyingly common slogan) and shamelessly publishes AI-written content. At least they’re honest about it. Some publications have deliberately tricked people; Sports Illustrated was caught publishing AI-written pieces by nonexistent journalists. Guest op-eds in all of the major newspapers have been found to be either partly or wholly written by AI. Sometimes publishing this work can happen inadvertently; here at Current Affairs, we have had plenty of freelance submissions that use suspicious numbers of em-dashes and “this is not an X, it’s a Y” sentences. (We can’t promise that nothing will ever slip through the cracks, but we’re vigilant!) Astonishingly, though, some editors have actually defended publishing the pieces even when writers have been caught. The Wall Street Journal published an op-ed from a hedge fund billionaire, Stan Druckenmiller, that turned out to have been AI-generated (probably because billionaires are inarticulate due to a lifetime of never having to craft arguments to persuade the yes-men around them), but the paper defended publishing the piece, since it reflected the billionaire’s genuine opinion.
The trends are dire. But it’s obvious why these publications are rushing to replace writers. They are for-profit corporations, whose ultimate loyalty is to shareholders, not workers. AI is great for them, because it can produce “content” at a fraction of the expense that a writer costs. In fact, on the Milton Friedman theory that the only responsibility a business has is to increase its profits, CEOs are obligated to replace writers with AI if doing so is better for the bottom line. It’s a simple calculation: if producing 100 posts with AI costs almost nothing and takes four minutes, but paying a writer to produce 20 posts costs $5,000, well, why would you pay the writer? The calculation might hold even if the quality drops substantially, errors are introduced, and audience loyalty plummets. Even if you lost 60 percent of your readership, you might still make a lot more per story, because you can pump them out in seconds.
Futurism reports that despite the common narrative that AI has not led to major job loss, creative industries are being “eviscerated” by AI, which is fueling “one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” with more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries being lost in four years. The situation is horrible for artists. Game studios are now designing their worlds and levels using “art assets generated with full AI workflows.” As Brian Merchant reported earlier this year:
Opportunities and pay rates declining as clients and employers embrace generative AI. Artists getting more touch-up jobs and fewer well-paying, sustainable gigs. Pessimism, anger, and even despair, growing common, if not universal, in the field.
This is especially galling given that all of the AI models that are being used to replace artists were trained through the mass theft of those very same artists’ work!
Now here at Current Affairs, we’ve decided to say: fuck that! Over 62 beautiful print issues, we have commissioned hundreds of original, handmade artworks from brilliant artists around the world. We’ve published meticulously researched and edited articles, which often take weeks or months to go from the draft stage to publication. We spend ages working on our page layouts, poring over photographs for the magazine, tweaking sketches, moving sentences around in articles. The labor that goes into this magazine has been extensive from the start, and most of it is hidden from view. We do it because we care about quality. If you pick up a copy of our magazine, you’ll see the result. I think it’s clear when you read it that we actually care about what we’re putting out. It’s not just Content designed to farm clicks.
Current Affairs has always been a bit of an anachronism. We started a print magazine in 2016. Nobody thought this was a good idea. (The editor in chief of Vanity Fair told me to my face that this was a wholly misguided project and certain to fail. I remain grateful to him for giving me the resolve to prove the prediction wrong.) Everyone else was pivoting to video. We pivoted to ink and paper, sent via the U.S. Postal Service. Ten years later, we are still here, while a lot of other places that began with a lot more money have folded (see, e.g., the Messenger, which burned through $50 million in a year and then died). The reason we’ve survived is that there are still many people who don’t like that all media is now just transient images on a social media feed. They experience a thrill when they get a cool thing in the mail that they can unwrap and hold. They know that seeing a beautiful illustration on the printed page is different, and better, from seeing it as a JPEG on your phone.
So we don’t really give a damn what the trends in the industry are. We located ourselves in New Orleans when everyone else is in New York. We defiantly publish on obscure topics that aren’t anywhere in the news cycle. (Have you read Alice Millar-Thompson’s article on eel smuggling?) And we’re going to keep paying human artists to create elaborate, gorgeous works of handmade art that take ages to make.
So our rule is simple: No AI generated articles or illustrations in the magazine! We are not going to feed you slop. And we think you should not give money to any publication that does feed you slop, because they’re both treating their audience with contempt, and avoiding paying workers so that their owners can get richer.
This doesn’t mean nobody doing work here can ever use any of the softwares that are broadly lumped together as AI. Much as we respect the Luddites around here, we’re not against technological innovation. Nothing in our rules prohibits writers from using a new tool to help them research something, or prevents an artist from using a tool to, say, add a texture or change a color, or make some kind of small element. But we need, first, to ensure that technologies are a tool used by workers to help them, rather than a tool used to replace workers. And, second, we need to make sure that readers aren’t being fed things that look like people’s genuine thoughts and creative expression but are in fact the product of disembodied mathematical formulas.
I’ll admit, I used to be excited by generative AI. I made goofy little images in DALL-E. I liked the dumb novelty songs. I thought it could be a cool tool for creative professionals to play around with. I forgot for a moment that we live under capitalism, where every new technology will be used by the ruling class to fuck over workers. As Garrison Lovely writes in his new book Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion Dollar Race to Replace Us—and How to Stop It, the developers of AI don’t see it as an asset for workers, but as a way to replace them. They’re trying to build a device whose success is literally measured by whether it successfully replaces people. It is not being designed to help the average person’s capacity to achieve their goals, but to help automate us all into obsolescence. That’s why it has to be fought aggressively.
We at Current Affairs are not capitalists. There are no profits to be made here. We’re a unionized 501c3 organization, which means that we have no incentive to try to replace our workers with machines. So we’re going to demonstrate that you don’t have to do this, that there’s another way, and that it results in better media that is more pleasurable to read and more informative. It’s not going to be easy, because competitor publications are going to be able to produce immense quantities of writing in the time we are painstakingly correcting and adjusting a single article.
But like John Henry, before we let that steam drill beat us, we will die with our hammer in our hand.
We need your help to keep putting out this handmade magazine. Subscribe or donate today. Your money pays real writers and real artists to make the world’s most beautiful printed publication. If you value authentic human thought and culture, get Current Affairs today.
articles.summary:
The magazine Current Affairs has implemented a strict anti-AI policy, banning all AI-generated text and illustrations to preserve human creativity and combat the automation of media production.

### Key Points
- The new policy, established through a union contract, prohibits the use of AI-generated content and art in the magazine.
- Current Affairs aims to counter the industry-wide trend of replacing human writers and artists with low-cost, automated content.
- Reports indicate that creative industries have lost over 200,000 jobs in four years, partly due to the adoption of generative AI workflows.
- The publication distinguishes between using AI as a minor assistive tool and using it to replace human labor or deceive readers.
- The magazine operates as a unionized 501(c)(3) organization, prioritizing human-led editorial processes over profit-driven automation.

### Why it Matters
This policy highlights a growing ideological divide in the media industry between profit-focused corporations and organizations prioritizing human labor. By rejecting AI-generated content, the publication challenges the market trend of prioritizing high-volume, low-cost output over editorial quality and worker sustainability.

articles.title: "Total War: Shogun 2 Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards", Sega say as they pull it from stores and restore the original
articles.author: Mark Warren
articles.content:
Total War: Shogun 2's Complete Edition is set to be pulled from stores by publishers Sega and developers Creative Assembly, who've admitted that it fell short of both player expectations and its creators' standards. The studio and their overlords have pledged to "investigate the issues" with the game and will be reinstating the original version of Shogun 2 as the purchasable one while they do so.
"We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards," the pair wrote in a statement posted to Steam and Sega's socials. "We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.
"As a result we are working with platform holders to remove the game from sale and to reinstate the original game while we investigate the issues. Existing owners will still be able to access and play the game. We are working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 – Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War."
The Complete Edition's Steam reviews currently sit at the overwhelmingly negative mark. There's some variety in the complaints, but the kicker is folks accusing Sega and Creative Assembly of having used generative AI to upscale the game's unit cards and not having disclosed that properly.
If those allegations turn out to be accurate, the complete edition will likely be sporting one or both of some new card art or an AI use disclosure whenever it makes its way back onto the store. If you'd already bought that version, you'll be able to keep on playing it from your library during its absence from sale, with the same having applied to the original while it was on vacation immediately following the complete edition's arrival on October 13th.
For a rundown of all the positive tweaks the complete ediion was supposed to make, here's some news on that from Edwin, who I bet's rather glad he didn't end up using it as an excuse to finally play Shogun 2 for the first time.
articles.summary:
Sega and Creative Assembly are removing Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition from digital storefronts following widespread player criticism regarding poor quality and undisclosed generative AI usage.

### Key Points
- Sega and Creative Assembly pulled the Complete Edition from sale after receiving overwhelmingly negative reviews on Steam.
- The original version of Total War: Shogun 2 will be reinstated as the primary purchasable option during the investigation.
- Players have specifically criticized the use of generative AI to upscale unit card artwork without proper disclosure.
- Existing owners of the Complete Edition retain full access to the game in their personal libraries despite its removal from stores.
- Developers are currently working with partners to identify technical issues and improve the product to meet established quality standards.

### Why it Matters
This decision highlights the growing tension between game developers and players regarding the implementation of generative AI in professional software. It serves as a cautionary example for publishers on the importance of transparency and quality control when updating legacy titles for modern audiences.

articles.title: Now generally available: Preview client-side encrypted PDF and image files directly in Google Drive
articles.author: Paul Jiménez Vela
articles.content:
October 15, 2026
Now generally available: Preview client-side encrypted PDF and image files directly in Google Drive
Client-side encryption (CSE) gives organizations ultimate control over who can access their most confidential data, using customer-managed encryption keys that render the data unreadable to unauthorized third parties, including Google. Google Drive now supports previewing CSE files directly within Drive. Previously, users had to download encrypted non-native files to their local devices in order to see the contents. With this capability, authorized users can preview encrypted content instantly in their web browser without ever leaving Drive.
The feature improves productivity and strengthens security by removing the need for unnecessary downloads. At launch, previewing is available only in Drive, and only for:
- Encrypted PDF documents
- Encrypted image file formats
Getting started
- Admins: There is no admin control for this feature.
- End users: This feature will be on by default. Visit the Help Center to learn more.
Rollout pace
- Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains: Extended rollout (potentially longer than 15 days for feature visibility) starting on October 15, 2026
Availability
- Enterprise: Enterprise Plus
- Education: Education Standard and Plus
- Other Editions: Frontline Plus, Assured Controls, Assured Controls Plus
Resources
- Google Workspace Admin Help: About client-side encryption
- Google Workspace Help Center: Get started with encrypted files in Drive, Docs, Sheets & Slides
- Google Workspace Updates Blog: Preview client-side encrypted PDF and image files directly in Google Drive, now available in beta
articles.summary:
Google Drive now allows users to preview client-side encrypted PDF and image files directly in their web browsers, eliminating the need to download sensitive documents for viewing.

### Key Points
- Google introduced native previewing for client-side encrypted (CSE) PDF and image files within the Drive interface.
- The feature removes the requirement to download encrypted files to local devices, enhancing both security and user productivity.
- This update is available by default for all authorized users with no additional administrative configuration required.
- The rollout began on October 15, 2026, for Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains.
- Availability is restricted to specific Google Workspace editions, including Enterprise Plus, Education Standard, and Assured Controls.

### Why it Matters
This update streamlines workflows for organizations handling highly confidential data by reducing the security risks associated with downloading sensitive files to local hardware. By keeping encrypted content within the browser environment, businesses can maintain stricter control over their information while improving operational efficiency for end users.

articles.title: Experts uncover bizarre new malware that spooks users with jump scares and screams
articles.author: Sead Fadilpašić
articles.content:
- KGB RAT is a malware-as-a-service platform offering remote access, credential theft, and crypto hijacking features
- The malware includes unusual psychological tactics such as fake BSODs, jump scares, and screamer functions
- Researchers found multiple operators using the tool, which is marketed as legitimate software despite its criminal capabilities
Halloween is just around the corner, and cybercriminals are making use of it to give Windows users a good scare (and then some!) - ater all, few things strike fear into the hearts of Windows users quite like the infamous Blue Screen of Death (BSOD), and a newly analyzed malware strain is turning that nightmare - into a weapon.
Security researchers Group-IB have published an in-depth report on KBG RAT, a newly discovered Remote Access Trojan (RAT). The malware has been advertised for sale on underground forums since late 2025, although researchers found evidence of its infrastructure dating back to January 2022. It’s quite possible that it was used privately for a little while before its developers decided to share it with the community.
KGB RAT
KGB RAT is offered as Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS), Group-IB explained, saying subscriptions start at $150 per month and reach $800 annually. The $150 package provides one month of access, while the $800 one covers the entire year, working out to roughly $67 per month for the annual subscription.
According to Group-IB, even the cheapest package includes all of the biggest features - remote desktop access, file management, webcam and microphone access, keylogging, password recovery, endpoint persistence, and different anti-detection features.
KGB RAT can also hijack cryptocurrency transactions by monitoring the clipboard for copied wallet addresses and replacing them with the ones owned by the attackers during pasting.
The more expensive plans, on the other hand, include multi-client management, payload customization, additional evasion features, plugin support, and access to more extensive server infrastructure. The unnamed developers are also offering a separate $500 Network Spreading add-on, which apparently allows the malware to propagate automatically throughout compromised networks.
Boo!
What makes this RAT stand out, however, are not its hacking features, but rather - thriller ones. In the report, Group-IB describes them as “a set of psychological harassment features”, which include screamer functions, jump scares, and forced blue screens of death. “Psychological harassment” might be a bit too harsh of a classification for a jump-scare during Halloween, but we would argue that what Microsoft did with its OS after Windows 11 could fall under that category.

KGB RAT’s developers call these features “fun settings”, the researchers discovered, while Group-IB says they’re a signal that the threat actor is “comfortable weaponizing victim anxiety alongside data theft”. Cryptocurrency theft, data exfiltration, keylogging, and remote desktop access, somehow seem to go hand-in-hand with anxiety, we believe.
The malware is designed to evade detection, using obfuscation, a reportedly daily-updated crypter, sandbox detection, and mechanisms for disabling (or simply bypassing) security protections. It uses a Telegram bot to notify the attackers when a new device becomes infected, and ip-api.com to determine where the compromised endpoint is located. The researchers said they identified multiple operators using the same malware builder, including at least one focused on stealing cryptocurrency from their victims.
Another interesting aspect of KGB RAT is that it is being positioned as a legitimate tool. Its website comes with (fake) customer reviews, and claims of being used by more than 10,000 IT professionals. It comes with an education section and different how-to videos. Ironically enough, the site was returning a “502 Bad Gateway” error when we tried to open it. While it could mean it was shut down, it can also mean a temporary server failure, or hosting problems, and it could make a comeback in the future.
While it was online, though, it contained a legal section with disclaimers, warnings and notifications encouraging users to make a legit use of their software, Group-IB found. They also included educational videos of how to install, configure, and use the software.

In his career, spanning more than a decade, he’s written for numerous media outlets, including Al Jazeera Balkans. He’s also held several modules on content writing for Represent Communications.

articles.summary:
Security researchers at Group-IB have identified KGB RAT, a sophisticated malware-as-a-service platform that combines traditional credential theft and crypto hijacking with unusual psychological harassment tactics for victims.

### Key Points
- KGB RAT is a Remote Access Trojan available via subscription models ranging from $150 monthly to $800 annually.
- Core features include remote desktop access, keylogging, file management, and automated cryptocurrency wallet address hijacking.
- The malware incorporates "fun settings" such as fake Blue Screen of Death (BSOD) errors, jump scares, and screamer functions.
- Developers offer a $500 network-spreading add-on to facilitate automatic propagation across compromised systems.
- The platform uses Telegram bots for infection notifications and employs advanced obfuscation to bypass security software.
- Operators market the tool as legitimate software, complete with fake customer reviews and instructional videos for users.

### Why it Matters
The emergence of KGB RAT highlights a growing trend where cybercriminals weaponize psychological distress alongside traditional data theft to maximize victim impact. By positioning malicious tools as legitimate software, developers are lowering the barrier to entry for inexperienced threat actors, increasing the overall risk to enterprise and personal network security.
